items.title: Why and how central banks emerged
items.core_explanation_md:
**Main stimulus:** the **need to finance wars**. Many early central banks were set up (and later **nationalised**) for **war finance**; after war, they turned to **mobilising resources for development** and **fighting inflation**.

**First functions:** **lender of last resort** and **monopoly of note issue** (one issuer makes the **quantity, quality and acceptability** of currency controllable and protects the **internal value of money**). Central banks also took charge of the **external value of money** (the exchange rate) to support **trade**.

**Early history (as the courseware states):** **Riksbank (Sweden, 1668)** is treated as the **first central bank** (a joint stock bank lending to the Government; **note issue monopoly in 1897**); the **Bank of England** and **Banque de France** were set up with **private capital** and helped sovereigns **finance their debt**. Nineteenth century bank dates: **France 1800**, **Finland 1811**, **Netherlands 1814**, **Austria and Norway 1816**, **Denmark 1818**, **Portugal 1846**, **Belgium 1850**, **Spain 1874**, **Germany 1876**, **Italy 1893**, **Japan 1882**.

**Widening role:** developing the **financial system**, **payment and settlement systems** (central banks provide **finality of settlement**), then **regulation and supervision** after bank failures, plus **risk management**. In **developing countries** (including India) post-colonial mandates grew to **development**, raising the risk of **fiscal dominance**. From the late twentieth century **price stability, financial stability and risk management** came to the fore.
items.expanded_explanation_md: War finance explains why many central banks started as government bankers.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The exigency of war financing.

items.title: Country histories: Bank of England, Banque de France, Bundesbank, Bank of Italy and the Federal Reserve
items.core_explanation_md:
| Bank | Key facts (courseware) |
| --- | --- |
| **Bank of England** | Founded **1694** (**William Paterson**'s scheme, **GBP 1.2 million** loaned to Government by subscribers); first an agency for **commercial banking**, **government banker and debt manager**; the **lender of last resort** after the **South Sea Bubble (1720s)**; **Bank Charter Act 1844** gave a **monopoly of note issue** in England and Wales; **nationalised 1946**; **operational independence on interest rates in 1997** |
| **Banque de France** | Established **1800**, with **private capital** and **state funds**; Governor and two Deputy Governors appointed by the Government; **15 regents** elected by the **200 largest shareholders**; note issue privilege (**Paris**, 15 years) extended to **all France in 1848**; **nationalised 1946**; **independence 1993**; **European System of Central Banks 1999** |
| **Banco de Portugal** | **Public limited company** in **1846**, a **note issuing commercial bank** |
| **Bundesbank** | Established **1957** (successor to the **Reichsbank, 1876-1945**); federal central bank integrating separate units; **part of the European System of Central Banks** |
| **Bank of Italy** | Founded **1893** after the near collapse of the banking system; part of the European System |
| **Federal Reserve** | Established **1913** after the **panic of 1907**; **dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices** (plus moderate long-term interest rates) |

**Federal Reserve structure:** a **Board of Governors** of **seven members** (**14-year terms**, nominated by the **President**, confirmed by the **Senate**), **twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks**, and the **FOMC** (**seven Governors plus twelve Reserve Bank presidents**, of whom **five** vote: the **New York Fed president** and **four rotating** on one-year terms). It is independent because its decisions need **no executive or legislative approval**, it gets **no Congressional funding** and **terms span several administrations**. After a **6 per cent dividend** on member bank capital and a surplus, **profits go to the Treasury**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Fed has both public and private elements: a government board and regional banks owned by member banks.

items.title: How the functions of central banks evolved
items.core_explanation_md:
**Milestones:** **paper money** issued by central banks replaced **full-value coins** around **World War I**; once notes were **legal tender** and **not convertible into gold**, central banks could control **money supply and prices**. After WWI they took on **supervision of commercial banks**, a firmer **lender of last resort** role, **credit to governments** and **debt management**, and used **open market operations** to fine-tune **interest rates and money supply**. Since **1933 (US)** and soon after **WWII (Germany)** central banks could impose **minimum reserve requirements**.

**Crises changed mandates:** the **Great Depression** added **monetary stability, full employment and growth**. Functions group into **monetary policy**, **banker to banks**, **banker to government** and **developmental** functions; **note issue and internal and external value of currency** are the key areas, with **growth promotion** added later.

**Financial stability** became an added objective, so **supervisory functions** grew; many central banks have **stopped financing their governments**.

**Moral hazard in last resort lending:** banks may behave **complacently** expecting **rescue**; central banks counter with **rigorous scrutiny** and by lending **at a penal rate**.

**Development role:** because **financial and economic development go together**, central banks run **credit policy**, **build institutions** and put in place **mechanisms to contain risks** from financial deepening.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Each crisis added a function: supervision after bank panics, reserve requirements after inflation, and stability after the 2008 crisis.

items.title: Reasons for proliferation and conflicting roles
items.core_explanation_md:
**Growth in number:** only about **a dozen** central banks in **1800**, but **over 160** now (courseware count). Reasons: **banking became complex**, **bank failures** made **regulation** necessary, and central banks **spread with nation states**.

**Why a central bank exists:** (1) an authority to run **note issue**; (2) an agency to be **banker and lender to the government**; (3) an agency to **regulate and supervise financial entities** and be **lender of last resort**.

**Conflicts of role:**

- **Banker or debt manager to Government vs price stability:** lending to the Government means **creating money**, risking **inflation**. This supports **central bank independence**, strengthened after the **Vietnam war** inflation and the **Latin American** episodes; **inflation targeting** (an **independent** bank pursuing a **target band**) became the main objective in many countries. A competing 'come of age' debate says central banks should not drop their 'parent', the **sovereign Government**.
- **Regulator and supervisor roles:** possible **conflict of interest**; by analogy with **Montesquieu's separation of powers** some countries moved supervision out of the central bank (the **UK Financial Services Authority, 2000**); in **India** the **Board for Financial Supervision** works **within the Reserve Bank**.

**Anchors:** price stability and the **external value** of currency relied on the **Gold Standard** and then the **dollar anchor**; the world lost its **anchor** on **15 August 1971** when the **US delinked the dollar from gold**.

**Modern core:** **development of financial markets and institutions**, **regulation and supervision**, **government debt management**, **payment and settlement systems** and the **external value** of currency; consensus that **inflation targeting** should be the **sole mandate** is **lacking**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The debate between independence and development roles shapes how each country designs its central bank.

items.title: Central banks in developed and developing countries
items.core_explanation_md:
| Feature | Developed countries | Developing countries |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Financial structure** | **Diversified and strong**; both **widening and deepening** | **Poor infrastructure**, **sparse banking network** |
| **Transmission** | **Smooth and fast**; interest rate changes pass through quickly | **Weak**; **informal markets** do not respond to policy signals |
| **Payments** | Mostly **cheques and drafts**; **currency to deposit ratio below about 10 per cent** | **Currency dominates**; **ratio as high as 80 per cent** in some; currency management is complex |
| **Origin of central bank** | Mainly **lender of last resort** | To **promote spread of commercial banks and credit flow**: a **developmental role** |
| **Instruments** | **Market based** (for example the **federal funds rate** as operating target 1970-79) | More **direct, sector specific tools** at first; must **develop financial markets** |
| **Autonomy** | High | Often limited, with **fiscal dominance** |

**Old vs transition economies:** transition economies can **start on a clean slate** and **graft systems** from developed countries; older developing countries must fit new frameworks to **existing systems**; a model must be **tailored to country features**.

**Role in developing countries:** a **facilitator** who builds **financial markets**, supports **smooth transmission**, meets **government financing needs** and promotes **socio-economic goals**.

**Recent events:** the **2008 global financial crisis** redefined mandates; the **Covid-19 pandemic** (a shock to **demand, supply and finance**) led central banks to use many measures to **support markets**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Developing country central banks often have to build the markets before they can use market tools.

items.title: Banker to government and public debt management
items.core_explanation_md:
**Role:** the central bank is the Government's **banker** and **agent** and, usually, its **debt manager**. The Government **keeps its accounts** with the central bank and **meets borrowing needs** by **placing bills** with it; the bank **issues notes** and **credits the Government's account**. This is **monetisation of government debt**: **more borrowing means more credit and more money**, which is **inflationary**.

**Constitutional position matters:** the **Bundesbank** has a **constitutional independence** so its support to government is **minimal** if there is a conflict; the **Bank of England** manages the Public Debt; in many **developing countries** the central bank gives **ways and means** or **ad hoc advances** against **government paper**.

**Fiscal-monetary co-ordination:** the Government's borrowing must not create **too much money**. Government securities are **backing for notes** and tools of **Open Market Operations (OMO)**: **buying** securities **adds** liquidity; **selling** **withdraws** it. Issuing debt to the **non-government sector** can **neutralise** liquidity but causes **crowding out** of private investment. A well-designed **borrowing programme** (spread of maturities) avoids **bunching**. If the market does not absorb the issue the central bank can **take up the surplus** and **sell it later**.

**Conflicts and separation:** the central bank may face **a dilemma** between **tightening liquidity** and **helping the borrowing succeed**, and **governments may press it to keep interest rates low**. The **agency view** favours a **separate debt management office** (**Germany, UK**: autonomous office; **Australia, France, US**: a separate office **under the Ministry of Finance**). Experience suggests combining debt management with monetary policy may **compromise price stability**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Monetisation links government deficits directly to money creation and inflation.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the monetisation of government debt?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The central bank issuing notes against government bills and crediting the Government account, creating money to finance the borrowing.

items.title: Banker to banks and lender of last resort
items.core_explanation_md:
**Banker to banks:** central banks keep **banks' reserves** and look after **financial stability**. Banks **create money** by lending: **loans become deposits** elsewhere, which allow **further lending** (**multiple credit creation**). The process carries **systemic risk**: **loss of faith in one bank** can spread to **sound banks** through **large withdrawals**, so the central bank must step in.

**Lender of last resort (LOLR):** a **banking crisis** is when **many banks** face **sudden demands** they cannot meet. The central bank provides **liquidity** (for example through the **discount window**) to **illiquid but solvent** banks, not to **insolvent** banks.

**History:** LOLR is **over 300 years old**; the **Bank of England** sometimes **suspended convertibility**; the **Federal Reserve** (1913) was created after repeated **booms, busts and banking crises**. The idea appears in **Thornton (1802)**, the term was coined by **Baring (1797)**, and **Bagehot (1873)** popularised it: lend **freely against good collateral at a high (penal) rate** to avert a systemic crisis and limit **moral hazard**.

**Moral hazard:** banks may take **excess risk** if they expect **cheap rescue**; a **penal rate** removes the incentive.

**Who bears losses?** Ultimately **society**, through **higher taxes or borrowing**. Lasting remedy means fixing the **root cause of NPAs** (industrial distortions, **fiscal imbalances**, structural problems) and keeping a **stable macroeconomic environment**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: LOLR is aimed at liquidity problems; insolvent banks are for resolution, not rescue loans.

self_check.prompt_text: To which banks should the lender of last resort lend according to the classical view in the courseware?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To illiquid but solvent banks, at a high rate.

items.title: Monetary policy function: base money, money multiplier and sources of monetary expansion
items.core_explanation_md:
**Backing for note issue** moved from **gold** to **government paper** and **foreign exchange reserves**.

**Sources of money supply change:**

- **Net central bank credit to government** (where **government liabilities exceed its deposits**, GL > GD);
- **Net foreign exchange reserves** (inflows add; outflows subtract);
- **Net central bank credit to the commercial sector**.

**Base money (reserve money, high powered money, RM):** **banks' balances with the central bank** (including the **CRR**) plus **cash in hand**. A rise in base money can expand money supply.

**Money multiplier:** **MM = Money Supply (MS) / Base Money (BM)**. Example in the courseware: **MM = 1.8** and **BM rises by Rs 2,000 crore** gives **MS up by Rs 3,600 crore**.

**Rationale:** banks are **both purveyors and creators of money**. Compliance with the CRR must be **enforced and penalised**, hence **central bank supervision**.

**Price stability** has become the **dominant objective**; **monetary policy committees**, **constitutional ceilings on public debt** and a **realistic approach** reinforce it. The central bank sets a **warranted rate of monetary expansion** each period; **credit policy** is an **adjunct** of monetary policy.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Control of base money and the multiplier gives the central bank a handle on broad money.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the money multiplier defined in the courseware?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The ratio of money supply to base money (high powered money).

items.title: Central bank digital currency (CBDC) and private digital currencies
items.core_explanation_md:
A **Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC)** is a **digital banknote**: a **liability of the central bank** (unlike **bank deposits**, which are **liabilities of commercial banks**). Central banks explore it to protect **public trust in money**, **price stability** and **safe, resilient payments**.

**Private digital currencies** (**Bitcoin, Litecoin, Ethereum, Ripple**) exist **only electronically** and are **not issued by a central bank**; they use **distributed ledger technology (DLT)** and the **blockchain**. The **Bank of England** judged they pose **no material risk** to **monetary or financial stability**.

**India (courseware, 2022):** the Reserve Bank launched the **Digital Rupee - Wholesale (e-Rs-W)** pilot on **1 November 2022** with **nine banks**, for **settlement of secondary market government securities trades**, expected to make the **inter-bank market more efficient** and **cut settlement costs** by removing the need for **settlement guarantee infrastructure or collateral**; the **retail pilot** began on **1 December 2022**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: CBDC extends central bank money to digital form for the public or for wholesale settlement.

self_check.prompt_text: Whose liability is a central bank digital currency?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The central bank.

items.title: Currency issue and management
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why central banks hold the monopoly:** with **many private issuers** there were **many currencies of varying acceptability**, **no control over quantity** and **loss of confidence**. The **government** entrusted note issue to the **central bank** for **uniformity**, **credibility** and **authenticity**.

**Currency management covers:** **notes and coins mix**, **design**, **printing**, **storage**, **distribution** and **disposal of soiled notes**; demand follows **monetary policy**.

**Backing:** early notes were **promissory notes** payable in **gold or silver**; under the **fractional reserve system** only a **fraction** needed backing, which allowed **over-issue**, so an **independent authority** was needed to **handle crises**, **limit issue** and ensure **credibility**.

**Country examples (courseware):** **Bank of France** (note privilege in **Paris** in **1803** for **15 years**, extended to **all France** in **1848**); **Banco de Portugal** (**monopoly in 1891**); **First Bank of the US** (**1789**) and **30,000 note varieties from 1600 banks by 1836**; **Greenbacks** (**1862**); **Bank of England** notes since **1694** (printing from **1855**); the **Fed** printing from **1913**. A **few central banks** (for example the **Monetary Authority of Singapore**) **do not issue notes**.

**Developed vs developing:** in **developed** countries **cheques and drafts** reduce the **share of currency**; **developing** countries rely on **currency** and face **high saving-investment gaps** and **deficits**, affecting issue.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A single trusted issuer is the basis of a uniform national currency.

self_check.prompt_text: Why was the note issue function entrusted to central banks?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To ensure uniformity, credibility and authenticity of currency and control of the quantity issued.

items.title: Payment and settlement systems
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why needed:** a transaction is not complete until **both payment and receipt are settled**; **failures in settlement hurt commerce**, so a **seamless system** is essential.

**History:** from **barter** to **money and banking**, then **cheques, drafts and electronic payments**; the earliest clearing was in **British Coffee Houses**, later **Clearing Houses**, whose volumes made **central banks take over** clearing to ensure **quick, safe settlement**. The **Giro system** grew out of the **postal system** in Europe (bank transfers on a Giro basis from the **mid-1960s**).

**Three organisational models:**

1. **Central bank** runs the **whole** function (regulatory and operational);
2. **Central bank regulates**, **private entities** operate clearing;
3. **Central bank regulates**; **clearing shared** between the central bank and **participating banks**.

**Examples:** **US**: the Fed regulates and also **processes cheques**; **UK, Canada, Sweden, Singapore, Malaysia, Hong Kong**: **private entities** clear.

**Large value systems (RTGS)** are usually **run by the central bank** because it is the **largest source of liquidity** and these payments affect **monetary policy operations**. Central banks **always do settlement** to achieve **settlement finality** and reduce **settlement risk**, while **letting go of clearing** to focus on **macroeconomic and liquidity management**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Settlement finality is the part central banks never delegate.

self_check.prompt_text: Which payment function do central banks retain even when they hand over clearing to private entities?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Settlement, to ensure finality.

items.title: Maintaining the internal value of currency: money, the gold standard and the Great Depression
items.core_explanation_md:
**Money's functions:** **medium of exchange**, **unit of account**, **standard of deferred payment** and **store of value**. **Inflation or deflation** damages the last two, **hurts the poor most**, and creates **uncertainty** that **reduces investment**: hence **price stability** is the core of monetary policy.

**Phases of price stability:** under the **gold specie standard**, **gold inflows and outflows** **adjusted the value of money automatically**. After the **gold standard was abandoned**, the **fiat standard** required central banks to **balance internal and external value** deliberately.

**Great Depression (1930s):** **Keynes** stressed **fiscal policy**; **Friedman and Schwartz** argued the **fall in money supply** caused by **contractionary central bank policies** and **bank failures** deepened it. The **Keynesian framework** also implied a **trade-off between inflation and growth** (the **Phillips curve**), which held **only in the short run**.

**Developing countries:** **saving-investment gaps** lead to **deficits** and **central bank money creation** (**seigniorage or inflation tax**); central banks then use **direct instruments** (**reserve requirements, selective credit control**) and **the SLR**, which makes **banks captive buyers of government securities**; the trend is **market-related rates** and **lower SLR**. The lesson: **pump-priming** does not raise real growth; **stable prices** are a **pre-condition** for growth.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Stable prices are a condition for growth, not a trade for it, over the medium term.

self_check.prompt_text: What is seigniorage, as the courseware describes it?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Raising resources for the budget gap through additional money creation, which works as an inflation tax.

items.title: Inflation targeting, monetary targets and anchors
items.core_explanation_md:
**Evolution:** in the **1970s and 1980s** policy centred on **money, output and prices**, and **monetary stock** became an **intermediate target**. **Money demand became unstable** with **financial innovation**, so many banks **dropped monetary targeting** in the 1980s (the **Bundesbank** kept it). Central banks may use **interest rates, exchange rates, monetary aggregates** or **multiple indicators**.

**Inflation targeting (IT):** the central bank, **in consultation with the Government**, announces a **numerical inflation target** for a **specified time**: a **point target** or a **band**. Early adopters (courseware): **New Zealand, Canada, UK, Finland, Israel, Spain, Sweden**. Benefits: a **domestic anchor**, **accountability**, **clearer inflation outlook**, **smaller inflation shocks** and **stable long-term interest rates**.

**Price stability vs a price level target:** with a **price level path** target the bank must **make up** for past misses; with an **inflation rate** target it need not.

**Pre-requisites:** the central bank is **not obliged to finance the budget**, has **effective market determined instruments**, **transparent practices**, **forecasting ability**; a **price index** such as the **CPI** is chosen. **Developing countries** have **higher inflation**, and **autonomy is constrained by fiscal needs**.

**Transmission lags:** the **longer the lag**, the **earlier** the bank must act. **Anchors** include **Reserve Money, money stock and multiple indicators**; **e-money** is value stored electronically on a device.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Inflation targeting trades discretion for a public commitment and accountability.

items.title: Maintaining the external value of currency and exchange rate regimes
items.core_explanation_md:
**Gold standard:** the exchange rate followed **specie flow**: **gold inflows** raised the money supply and **outflows** reduced it. **Purchasing power parity** explains rates by **equalising purchasing power**; **mercantilist** policy aimed for **trade surpluses** with a **depressed exchange rate**.

**Timeline (courseware):**

| Event | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| **Gold standard collapse** | After **World War I**; UK returned **1925**, left **1931**; US left **1933**; **beggar-thy-neighbour devaluations 1929-30** |
| **Bretton Woods (1944)** and the **IMF** | **Dollar as pivot currency**; parities held within **1 per cent** either side; changes only for **fundamental disequilibrium** |
| **SDRs (1967)** | Introduced by the IMF after the **pound sterling devaluation** to manage **global liquidity** |
| **Smithsonian Agreement (1971)** | Group of Ten; **band widened to 2.25 per cent** either side; the UK floated sterling in **June 1972** |
| **Floating (1972-73)** | UK floated **June 1972**; by **March 1973** a **'non-system'** |
| **ERM collapse (early 1990s)** | Pegs to the **DM** or **Sterling** could not be sustained |
| **East Asian crisis (1997)** | **Thailand** abandoned the baht peg in **July 1997**; contagion to **Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia** |

**Impossible trinity:** a **fixed exchange rate**, **full capital convertibility** and **independent monetary policy** cannot be had together. A **currency crisis** is a **loss of confidence**, driven by **expectation that a peg is unsustainable**; successful pegs need **low capital mobility**, **high trade share with the anchor**, **similar shocks** and **strong fundamentals**. Exchange rate regimes are usually **managed** (**de jure vs de facto**).

**Asia lessons:** **appropriateness of pegs**, **balanced deregulation**, **close monitoring of short-term debt**, **liquidity management**, **data dissemination** and **timely IMF support**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A central bank cannot have a fixed exchange rate, open capital account and its own interest rate policy at the same time.

self_check.prompt_text: What does the impossible trinity say cannot be achieved at the same time?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A fixed exchange rate, full capital convertibility and independent monetary policy.

items.title: Regulation and supervision of the financial system, Basel framework and structure of supervision
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why central banks regulate:** banks use **public deposits** to fund **credit**; failures cause **systemic damage**; central banks protect **depositors** and set **rules of business**. Banks' **balance sheets** matter for monetary management: **asset-liability mismatches** (long assets, short liabilities) can cause **runs**; **off-balance-sheet items** must be **transparent**.

**Supervision:** it **limits depositors' losses**, keeps **public confidence**, and has **micro-prudential** (on-site and off-site) and **macro-prudential** parts; supervisors now stress **macro-prudential** work as the distinctions between **banks and other institutions** blur and **universal banking** grows.

**Approach:** supervisors judge **how much risk**, **what resources** (capital, liquidity, management quality) and **whether resources are sufficient**; the **CAMELS** approach (**Capital, Assets, Management, Earnings, Liquidity, Interest rate Sensitivity**) led to **risk based supervision (RBS)**: **differentiated** supervision (Bank of England 1997, Canada 1999, Australia 2000, **RBI**: two pilot rounds for **23 banks**, new rating framework in **October 2005**).

**Basel Core Principles (2012):** **29 principles** (first **25 in 1997**, revised **2006, 2012**): **Principles 1-13** on **supervisors' powers, responsibilities and functions**; **14-29** on **prudential regulations and requirements** (governance, risk management, capital adequacy, credit, problem assets, concentration, related parties, country risk, market, interest rate, liquidity, operational, internal control and audit, reporting, disclosure, abuse of financial services).

**Basel II (2005): three pillars:** **minimum capital** (credit, market, operational risk), **supervisory review** and **market discipline**. **Basel III (December 2010):** better **quality and level of capital**, a **leverage ratio**, improved **liquidity framework**, **capital conservation buffer** and **countercyclical buffer**, and a **macro-prudential** focus.

**Structure of supervision:** **unified** (**economies of scale and scope**, **financial conglomerates**, **accountability**, **competitive neutrality**) vs **separate** (to avoid **moral hazard** and conflicts; UK **FSA**); after the **2008 crisis** responsibilities moved back to the Bank of England (**Financial Stability Committee**) and the US **Dodd-Frank** placed them with a **committee chaired by the Treasury Secretary**. A **'super regulator'** covers **banks, securities and insurance**; the courseware says **specialist regulators work well in emerging markets**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Basel II adds supervisory review and market discipline to minimum capital; Basel III adds buffers, leverage and liquidity.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the three pillars of Basel II.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Minimum capital requirements, supervisory review and market discipline.

items.title: Financial stability, promotional functions, market development and communication
items.core_explanation_md:
**Financial stability:** **Mishkin**: a system that ensures **efficient allocation of savings to investment** without major disruption. **Y.V. Reddy:** **uninterrupted transactions**, **confidence**, and **no excessive volatility** affecting the real economy. After the **gold standard** and the **fiat money** era, policy focused on **price stability**; **interest in financial stability returned** in the **late 1980s**, and its risk rose in the **1990s** with **technology** and **blurring of sectors**. Central banks provide **emergency liquidity**, rely on **financial markets** for monetary transmission and **oversee payment systems**. **Monetary stability does not guarantee financial stability** (stable conditions can breed **excess optimism**; **asset price booms**: 'irrational exuberance'). **Precautionary measures:** **standards and codes**, **prudential regulation**, **early warning signals**, **supervision**, **capital adequacy norms**, **asset classification**, **income recognition**, **market valuation** and **NPA recovery**.

**Promotional functions:** in developing countries the central bank also acts as a **developmental bank**: **sector credit** (including **selective credit**, **credit subsidies**) as **quasi-fiscal activity**; but the **inflation-growth trade-off** holds only in the **short run**.

**Market and institution development:** developing countries have **thin, oligopolistic markets**; central banks help the Government with **public debt** or **seigniorage**, build **money, bond, forex and capital markets**, set up **deposit insurance** and **credit guarantee** schemes, and found **development finance institutions** (the **Reserve Bank** set up **IDBI** and **NABARD**).

**Communication:** monetary and credit policy statements, reports; **'monetary mystique'** and **'constructive ambiguity'** were older styles; with **inflation targeting** and greater independence, **transparent, tailored communication** shapes **expectations** and reduces **spill-over risk**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Clear communication helps policy work by guiding public expectations.

items.title: Autonomy and independence of a central bank
items.core_explanation_md:
**History:** central banks began as **private** institutions, **independent of government** until the **Second World War**; around WWII **Germany, France, England, Japan, Italy and Sweden** subordinated them to governments; experience since has shown banks **work best when autonomous** and that **low inflation** is more attainable.

**Revival of interest** came from **reforms in planned economies**, the new **European Central Bank (ECB)** and the need for **price stability** amid **cross border capital flows**.

**Arguments for independence:** governments are **myopic** and drift to **inflationary policy** for short-run gains; the more the bank **supports public debt**, the more **pressure on liquidity management**; an independent bank can take the **long view**.

**Recent milestones (courseware):** **Bank of England** legally independent in **June 1998**; **Bank of Japan** gained **operational (not legal) independence in April 1998**; **ECB** operational in **June 1998** and the **most independent** because it is **supranational**.

**Three dimensions of independence:**

| Dimension | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Personnel** | Appointment of officials, **term of office**, **dismissal rules**; in **over two-thirds** of banks surveyed by the BIS at least **two political bodies** were involved in proposing and appointing |
| **Financial** | Freedom from **automatic monetisation** of deficits; the **bank's own budget** |
| **Policy** | **Goal independence** (bank sets its own goals) vs **instrument independence** (bank chooses instruments for goals set by law) — most banks have **instrument but not goal independence** |

**Evidence:** studies link independence with **lower average inflation**, especially under **Bretton Woods**; in the **1990s** the link was **harder to see**; the **correlation may be endogenous**; **New Zealand** (**independence and a clear mandate in 1988**) took inflation from **double digits to under 2 per cent**. **Critics:** it lacks **democratic legitimacy**; but banks stay **answerable to the legislature**.

**Preconditions:** **transparency about aims**, **accountability to the legislature** and **credibility to overcome time inconsistency**. **Time inconsistency** arises when the bank **abandons its own policy** (for example expanding money to **accommodate wage settlements**); the cures are **no discretionary reneging** or a **fixed rule**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Independence works best when paired with transparency and accountability.

self_check.prompt_text: What is goal independence?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The central bank sets its own objectives rather than having them set by law.

items.title: Credibility and accountability of a central bank
items.core_explanation_md:
**Credibility:** a **track record** of low inflation shapes **public expectations**; if people trust the bank, **inflation expectations stay low** and **prices and wages follow**; if not, they **build inflation into their plans** and policy becomes **ineffective**. **Time (dynamic) inconsistency** erodes credibility when the bank **fails to stick to its promises** under **pressure to support public debt**. Remedies: **independence**, **inflation targeting regimes** that **hold the central bank responsible** for missing targets, and **instruments that limit surprises**.

**Accountability** means **responsibility for policy actions**; together with **autonomy and transparency** it supports **price and financial sector stability**. Measures: the **Briault, Haldane and King index** (parliamentary monitoring, **minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee**, **policy reports**, an **override mechanism**) and the **Fry index** (accountability for a **specific target** and **public accountability**). **Nolan and Schaling:** accountability implies **some compromise** of independence; **De Haan:** that depends on the **measure**; in the long run both **can co-exist**. Even the **Fed** is accountable: the **Chair testifies to Congress**.

**Ways to ensure accountability:** **clear goals** (a **single numerical price stability objective** helps, but excluding all other goals is **not desirable**); a **reappointment process**; reviews of **decisions, budget and spending**; **testimony to the legislature**; a **supervisory board** approving the bank's **budget**; and **publication** of **annual reports, inflation reports and MPC minutes**.

**Bank of England example:** if inflation misses the target by **more than one percentage point** in either direction, the **Governor (for the MPC)** must **write an open letter to the Chancellor**, explaining the cause and how long it will take to **return to target**; the MPC **publishes a quarterly inflation report**.

**Transparency best practices:** **official reports** analysing the economy, **forecasts of key variables with risks**, and **reasons for decisions**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Accountability is the democratic counterpart of independence.

self_check.prompt_text: When must the Governor of the Bank of England write an open letter to the Chancellor, as the courseware states?
self_check.expected_takeaway: When inflation misses the target by more than one percentage point, above or below.

items.title: Transparency and key international standards and codes
items.core_explanation_md:
**Definition:** transparency is the **absence of asymmetric information** between policy makers and other agents, **reducing uncertainty**. It is needed because of **financial crises caused by information gaps**, **integrated markets**, **greater autonomy and accountability** and the **stress on financial stability**. It is a **secondary but important objective**: the bank is an **agent** answerable to the public (**principal-agent** relationship). **Disclosure** deters **discretionary policy**, **time inconsistency** and **excess risk taking**, and makes **policy more effective** if the public **understands the goals and instruments**.

**International initiatives:** began at the **1995 Halifax Summit (G-7)**; after the **East Asian crisis**, in **April 1998** finance ministers and central bank Governors set up **three working groups**: **transparency and accountability**, **strengthening domestic financial systems**, **managing international financial crisis**.

**IMF Code of Good Practices on Transparency in Monetary and Financial Policies (March 2000)** and the **ELRIC** framework (**E**xternal audit mechanism, **L**egal structure and independence, financial **R**eporting, **I**nternal audit mechanism and a system of internal **C**ontrol); the IMF **safeguards assessment** is a **diagnostic** of these five areas.

**Twelve key standards (after the 1994 Mexican crisis, Task Force chaired by Andrew Sheng):**

| Area | Standard | Body |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monetary and financial policy transparency | **Code of Good Practices** | **IMF** |
| Fiscal transparency | **Code of Good Practices on Fiscal Transparency** | **IMF** |
| Data dissemination | **SDDS / GDDS** | **IMF** |
| Insolvency | **Principles and Guidelines on Effective Insolvency and Creditor Rights System** | **World Bank** |
| Corporate governance | **Principles of Corporate Governance** | **OECD** |
| Accounting | **International Accounting Standards** | **IASB** |
| Auditing | **International Standards on Auditing** | **IFAC** |
| Payment and settlement | **Core Principles for Systemically Important Payment Systems** | **CPSS-BIS** |
| Market integrity | **Forty Recommendations (money laundering)** | **FATF-OECD** |
| Banking supervision | **Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision** | **BCBS** |
| Insurance supervision | **Insurance Core Principles** | **IAIS** |

**Credibility** is an **intangible asset**, hard to measure, but shown by a **track record** of achieving **price stability**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Standards and codes spread common transparency and supervision practices across countries.

self_check.prompt_text: What does the E in the ELRIC framework stand for?
self_check.expected_takeaway: External audit mechanism.

items.title: Conflict with fiscal policy: history, theory and global experience
items.core_explanation_md:
**Origin of conflict:** early central banks were set up to **finance governments**; with **note issue monopoly** and the role of **government banker**, the **owner (government) became the bank's principal debtor**; **unmitigated access** to central bank credit **eroded the currency's value** and hindered **monetary stability**.

**Theory:**

- **Keynes** linked money and the real sector through **interest rate and investment**; for two decades after WWII **fiscal policy** took centre stage (Depression, reconstruction).
- The **1970s** (collapse of fixed exchange rates, **oil shock**, bad harvests, Vietnam war) produced **stagflation**: **no long-run trade-off** between inflation and unemployment.
- **New-classical economists** (**rational expectations**, market clearing): **only unanticipated policy has real effects, and only temporarily**; prefer **rules** over **discretion**.
- **Keynesians** replied that anticipated policy can matter if markets do not clear; **fiscal policy** is **not agile** (political influence) and amounts to **another demand shock** monetary policy must offset; so **independent central banks** (the **Bundesbank**, later the **ECB**) were favoured.
- **Game theory (1980s):** **non-cooperation** between fiscal and monetary authorities gives **sub-optimal outcomes**; **coordination** stressed since the **mid-1980s**.

**Fiscal responsibility legislation** (limits on central bank accommodation and borrowing ceilings) frees monetary policy; some countries with **hyperinflation** history legislated **central bank autonomy**.

**Emerging economies:** central banks watch the **fiscal position** because **deficit size and financing** drive **interest rates and prices**; **foreign financing** of public debt is **limited**, so **domestic financing** dominates; deficit financing by the central bank risks a **debt trap** (borrowing to repay earlier debt); **market borrowing** instead risks **crowding out private investment**; central banks hold government securities as **backing for currency** and for **OMOs**; large government absorption of liquidity **constrains bank lending** and **pushes up interest rates**.

**Market borrowing programme and primary dealers (PDs):** the Government announces its **annual borrowing** in the budget; participants: **RBI, commercial banks, other financial institutions, individuals and PDs**. **PDs** are **registered market makers** and **underwriters**; the unsubscribed portion that falls to them is **devolvement**. **Private placement** with the central bank is a **temporary form of monetisation**; **direct monetisation** (India: **ad hoc Treasury Bills from the mid-1950s to March 1997**) is rarely preferred. The central bank tries to **offload privately placed securities quickly** (liquidity injection through **refinancing, foreign exchange absorption or repos**), though that adds to demand and prices. In **EMEs** the **secondary market is thin**, so banks prefer **lending** to holding securities above the **SLR**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Coordination and legal limits on central bank financing are the practical answers to the conflict.

self_check.prompt_text: What is devolvement as the courseware describes it?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The absorption by primary dealers, as underwriters, of the part of a government securities issue that other participants do not take up.

items.title: Indian experience with debt management and separation of debt management
items.core_explanation_md:
**Concern in 1957:** the Reserve Bank warned that creation of **ad hoc Treasury Bills** to keep the Government's **weekly closing balance** had become a **mechanical process** with **no check on spending**, undermining its **statutory duty** to secure **monetary stability**.

**Ad hoc Treasury Bills:** originated in **World War II** (financing **sterling debt repatriation**), used again in **1948-49** for the **sterling balance agreement**; from **March 1955** an arrangement **automatically** created them to restore the Government's cash balance; they were **funded** into **undated special securities at 4.6 per cent from 1982**.

**Ending automatic monetisation:**

- **9 September 1994** First Supplemental Agreement: **limits on ad hocs** during **1994-95 to 1996-97**, then **phase out from April 1997**.
- **6 March 1997** Supplemental Agreement: **ad hocs completely phased out**; replaced from **1 April 1997** by **Ways and Means Advances (WMA)**: **short-term advances repayable within three months**.
- The Reserve Bank can **float fresh government securities** when **75 per cent of the WMA limit** is reached; **overdraft** beyond the limit carries an **interest rate higher than WMA**.

**1960s conflicts:** the Reserve Bank used an **incremental CRR in 1960** because it could not raise the **Bank Rate**; the Bank Rate moved **4 to 6 per cent in 1960-66**; it became a **net purchaser of government securities** to steady markets.

**Separating debt management from monetary policy:** the Government would **fully fund the deficit from the public at market rates**, **taking debt management out of the central bank**; it would decide **size, instruments (bonds, bills, indexed), currency, timing, maturity and coupon**; the central bank would still **advise on size and timing** (it tracks liquidity), **process tenders**, **maintain the registry** and provide **clearing and settlement**. **New Zealand** set up a separate office in the **late 1980s**; **Ireland, Sweden, Australia and the UK** followed. Reasons for separation: avoid an **insider information problem** (monetary policy tailored to help debt operations) and keep **accountability** clear; if not separated, **allocate and define responsibilities separately**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: India replaced automatic monetisation with a limited, temporary facility, a clear policy decision to protect monetary control.

self_check.expected_takeaway: 1 April 1997.

items.title: Evolution of the Reserve Bank and the idea of a central bank in India
items.core_explanation_md:
**Early attempts:** the **General Bank of Bengal and Bihar (1773)** under **Warren Hastings** (short-lived); later **proposals** (**1807-08, 1836, 1860**) stayed on paper.

**Presidency Banks:** **Bank of Calcutta (1806)** became **Bank of Bengal (1809)**; **Bombay (1840)** and **Madras (1843)**; they were **quasi-government**, with **Government Directors** and part Government capital. The **Paper Currency Act (1862)** gave **note issue to the Government**.

**Pressure for a central bank:** the **Home Charges** (**sterling payments** by Government for debt, pensions and the War Office) made the **exchange rate** a budget issue; the **Fowler Committee**, **Rothschild's evidence** and **Keynes** pushed the idea; the **Chamberlain Commission (1913)** proposed **merging the three Presidency Banks**, which became the **Imperial Bank of India (1921)**, doing **banker to government** and partly **banker's bank** but **not** note issue or **foreign exchange**.

**Hilton Young Commission (1926)** recommended ending the **dichotomy** between **currency and credit control** and created the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**; Bill of **1927** failed over constitution; fresh **Bill passed in 1934**. The **RBI Act, 1934** took effect from **1 January 1935** (courseware), the **Bank began operations on 1 April 1935** as a **shareholders' bank**, and was **nationalised on 1 January 1949** under the **Reserve Bank (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948**.

**Core functions:** **issue of currency**, **banker to government** (including **debt management**), **banker to commercial banks**. **Preamble:** regulate **note issue** and **keep reserves** to secure **monetary stability** and operate the **currency and credit system** to the country's advantage. From the start the RBI also had a **promotional role** in **agricultural credit** (the **Agricultural Credit Department**, 1935).

**Exchange rate history:** the rupee was linked to **sterling** until **September 1975**, then to a **basket** until **1991**; a **dual rate** (**March 1992 to February 1993**) led to a **market-based system in March 1993**. **Exchange Control** began on **3 September 1939**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The RBI combined note issue, government banking and bankers bank functions with an early developmental task.

items.title: The developmental role: institutions, nationalisation and credit planning
items.core_explanation_md:
**Institutions the RBI promoted (courseware):** **IFCI (1948)**, **State Financial Corporations (1951)**, **ICICI (1955)**, **IDBI (1964)**, **UTI (1964)**, **Agricultural Refinance Corporation (1963)** → **Agricultural Refinance Development Corporation (1974)** → **NABARD (1982)**, **NHB (1988)**, **DFHI (1988)**, **IDFC (late 1990s)**, **primary dealers (late 1990s)**, **CCIL (2001)**, **BPSS (2005)**, **BCSBI (2006)**, **NPCI**, the **Deposit Insurance Corporation (1962)** and the **Credit Guarantee Corporation of India (1971)**.

**Banking expansion:** the **Imperial Bank** became **State Bank of India in July 1955**; **14 banks were nationalised in 1969** and **6 more in 1980** to align banking with **national goals** and take credit to **agriculture, small industry and rural areas**. Public sector bank branches rose from **8,262 (1969)** to **86,311 (2021)**; rural branches from **1,833** to **28,828** (dated figures, not taught).

**RBI response to nationalisation:** **credit planning** and the **Credit Planning and Banking Development Cell (1970)**; the **Lead Bank Scheme (1969)**; monitoring **priority sector** credit; the **Rural Banking Enquiry Committee (1949)** and **All-India Rural Credit Survey (1951)**; the **Department of Banking Development (1950)**; **Industrial Finance Department (1957)**; the **Banking Companies Act, 1949** (renamed **Banking Regulation Act, 1966**) and the **1950 and 1959 amendments** extending the Act's coverage to branches abroad and foreign branches; non-banking supervision created in **March 1966**.

**Context:** the **Planning Commission** and the **First Five Year Plan (1951)** made **financial development a tool for plan priorities**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The RBI built institutions to deliver credit that commercial banks alone did not provide.

items.title: Payment and settlement systems and cyber security
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why:** an efficient payment and settlement system is **essential for a modern financial sector**. India had used **hundis** (the credit instrument) for centuries.

**Clearing history:** **clearing houses** in the **Presidency towns** (19th century) → settlement via the **Imperial Bank (1921)** → **RBI took over** after **1935**.

**Reform programme:** committees (**Rangarajan I and II**, **Saraf**, **Patil**) and **Payment System Vision** documents from **1998** (latest to **December 2025**); recent steps: **RBI Innovation Hub**, **security of card transactions**, **limiting customer liability**, **Prepaid Payment Instruments**, **Online Dispute Resolution**, **system audit of PSOs**, **QR code** streamlining, **perpetual authorisation** for PSOs and the **RBI Digital Payments Index**.

**Systems:** **RTGS** (operationalised **March 2004**; **24x7 from 14 December 2020**; minimum **Rs 2 lakh**), **NEFT** (**24x7 from December 2019**), **IMPS** (24x7 instant), **APBS** (Aadhaar-seeded bulk **government benefit** payments, run by **NPCI**), **AEPS** (**biometric** Aadhaar payments) and **RuPay**. **CCIL** clears **money, government securities and forex** trades; the RBI keeps **settlement and oversight**.

**Cyber security framework (June 2016):** a **Board-approved cyber security policy** separate from the IT policy; a **Security Operations Centre (SOC)** for **continuous surveillance**; **network and database security**; **customer information protection**; a **cyber crisis management plan**; **preparedness indicators**; **reporting incidents to the RBI**; **gap assessment**; and **awareness**. The RBI also **examines IT and cyber security** and feeds this into **risk based supervision**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Payment systems and cyber security are now core supervisory topics because failure spreads quickly.

self_check.prompt_text: Which Board-approved document must banks have, distinct from their IT policy, under the 2016 RBI cyber security framework?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A cyber security policy, supported by a Security Operations Centre.

items.title: Relationship with the Government and the monetary-fiscal interface
items.core_explanation_md:
**Ownership and control:** the RBI is **fully owned by the Central Government**. **Section 7(1)** lets the Government give **directions in the public interest** after **consulting the Governor**; subject to that, the **Central Board** controls the affairs (**Section 7(2)**). The RBI is **banker to Central and State Governments** by **statute and agreements**.

**Monetisation history:** with **planning from 1951** the RBI helped **bridge the Government's resource gap** by **financing government debt** through **monetisation** and keeping **government security yields artificially low**. **Section 17** allows **advances to the Government repayable within three months** for **cash management**, but in practice **ad hoc Treasury Bills** created **automatic monetisation** from the **1950s to the 1990s**, so the RBI **lost control over reserve money**.

**Fiscal-monetary-inflation nexus:** by the late **1980s** excess monetary expansion fed **inflation**; the RBI **raised reserve ratios**; the Government borrowed from **captive sources** at **administered rates**: **financial repression**.

**Reforms:** early **1990s** shift to **fiscal stabilisation**; **9 September 1994** First Supplemental Agreement set **limits on ad hocs** for **three years**; **6 March 1997** Supplemental Agreement **phased out ad hocs** (replaced by **Ways and Means Advances**); the RBI stopped taking part in **primary auctions from 1 April 2006** under the **FRBM Act, 2003**; **SLR was lowered**; **interest rates were deregulated**.

**Debt management debate (Box 4.1):** the **Tarapore Committee (1997)** and the **Advisory Group on Transparency (2000)** favoured **separating debt management** from monetary policy; in India the RBI instead set up a **Financial Markets Department (2005)** to **separate operations functionally**; **monetary policy statements** are announced **bi-monthly** after considering the **Government's market borrowing**; a **Short-Term Liquidity Forecasting Model** projects **net liquidity daily**. Coordination resembles the **US Treasury-Federal Reserve** arrangement.
items.expanded_explanation_md: India separated the functions inside the RBI rather than moving debt management out of it.

self_check.expected_takeaway: 6 March 1997.

items.title: Structure and governance of the Reserve Bank in the early years
items.core_explanation_md:
**Origins of the governance structure:** the **Hilton Young Commission (1926)**, the **Indian Central Banking Enquiry Committee (1931)**, the **White Paper on Constitutional Reforms (1933)** and the **India Office Committee (1933)** (which recommended a **shareholders' bank** to avoid **political interference**) led to the **1934 Act**.

**Original Central Board:** a **Governor**, **two Deputy Governors** (appointed by the Governor General in Council), **four nominated directors**, **eight elected directors** (by shareholders) and **one Government official without a vote**; the **Governor and Deputy Governors were whole-time**. The **Government could supersede the Board** and **dismiss the Governor** without giving reasons. **Five Local Boards** were reduced to **four** by **the 1947 Amendment** (after the **Burma Monetary Arrangement ended**). The Board met **at least six times a year, once a quarter**; the **Governor presided** with a **casting vote**.

**Start:** **first Board meeting 14 January 1935, Calcutta**; operations began **1 April 1935** (first day of the fiscal year, for **changeover of Government accounts** from the Imperial Bank); **Central Office moved from Calcutta to Bombay in December 1937**.

**Early structure:** **Central Office** (Secretary's Section; Chief Accountant's Section with **Issue** and **Banking Departments**), the **Agricultural Credit Department**, the **Inspection Department (1935)**, the **Exchange Control Department (1939)**, **Department of Research and Statistics (1945)**. **Sir C.D. Deshmukh** became the **first Indian Governor on 11 August 1943** (till **June 1949**).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The shareholders bank model was meant to protect the central bank from political interference.

self_check.prompt_text: Who was the first Indian Governor of the Reserve Bank, and in which year did he take office?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Sir C.D. Deshmukh, on 11 August 1943.

items.title: Organisational developments and major departments
items.core_explanation_md:
**Supervision milestones:** the **Department of Supervision (1993)** became the executive arm of the **Board for Financial Supervision (BFS, 1994)**, chaired by the **Governor**, with **four non-official directors** and **Deputy Governors** as ex-officio members (the supervision DG is **Vice-Chairman**); in **July 1997** **DoS** became the **Department of Banking Supervision** and the **Department of Financial Companies** the **Department of Non-Banking Supervision**.

**Monetary policy:** the **Credit Planning Cell** became the **Monetary Policy Department from 1 January 1998**; under Governor **Bimal Jalan** policy shifted to **responsive** rather than periodic; **quarterly reviews** from **2005-06**; a **Technical Advisory Committee**. The **Financial Markets Department** (**2005**) and **Internal Debt Management Department** (**1992 cell**) separated markets and debt work.

| **Financial Markets Operations** (carved out **November 2014**) | **LAF (repo, reverse repo, MSF)**, **OMO**, **MSS**, **forex operations**, **NEER/REER** |

items.title: The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934: structure and salient features
items.core_explanation_md:
**Chapters:** **I** (Sections 1-2) preliminary; **II** (3-19) incorporation, capital, **management** (Central Board, Local Boards, disqualifications, meetings) and **business the Bank may or may not transact**; **III** (20-45) **central banking functions** (Government business, **note issue**, **foreign exchange**, **cash reserves of scheduled banks**); **III A** (45A-45G) **credit information**; **III B** (45H-45QB) **non-banking institutions receiving deposits**; **III C** (45R-45T) **unincorporated bodies' deposits**; **IV** (46-58A) **general provisions** (funds, **Bank Rate publication**, surplus, regulations); **V** (58B-58G) **penalties**. **Schedules:** **First** (the four areas for Local Boards) and **Second** (**scheduled banks**).

**Central Board:** a **Governor** and up to **four Deputy Governors**; **four non-official directors** (one from each Local Board); **ten non-official directors** nominated by the Government; **two Government officials** (from **1 February 2012**). The Government can **remove** the Governor, a Deputy Governor or any director, and **supersede the Board** by notification if the Bank fails its obligations (a report to **Parliament within three months**). The Board meets **at least six times a year and once each quarter**.

**Local Boards:** one for each of the **four areas**, **five members** each, **four-year term**, advise the Central Board.

**Note issue (Section 22):** the RBI is the **sole authority**; **rupee coins and one-rupee notes** are issued by the **Government** but circulate **only through the RBI**. The **Issue Department** is **separate** from the **Banking Department** and its assets (**gold, foreign securities, rupee coin and rupee securities**) must at least equal its liabilities (**notes in circulation**).

**Cash reserve (Section 42):** each **scheduled bank** keeps an **average daily balance** at a **notified percentage** of its **demand and time liabilities** (the fortnight runs **Saturday to the second following Friday**); additional balances may be prescribed; **penal interest** of **3 per cent above the Bank Rate**, **5 per cent** if the shortfall continues.

**Other provisions:** **credit information** (**Section 45D**); **Bank Rate** (**Section 49**); **Agricultural Credit Department** (**Section 54**); **weekly accounts** of the Issue and Banking Departments; **annual accounts** within **two months**, signed by the **Governor, Deputy Governors and Chief Accounting Officer**; the **Companies Act does not apply**; the Bank can be **liquidated only by Government order**; funds: **National Rural Credit (LTO and Stabilization)**, **National Industrial Credit (LTO)** and **National Housing Credit (LTO)**.

**Functions in the Act:** **banker to government**, **issue of notes**, **banker to banks** and **maintaining the exchange rate**; credit facilities under **Section 17**; credit control by **LAF-repo**, **Bank Rate** and **OMOs**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Act ties the Bank to the Government through directions and the Board but protects day-to-day administration from influence.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Three per cent above the Bank Rate.

items.title: The Banking Regulation Act: need, coverage and principal sections
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why it was needed (wartime banking):** **indiscriminate branch opening**, **unsound deposit-attracting methods**, **interlocking** of banks with **insurance and industrial concerns**, **dressing up of accounts** and **dubious devices** to enter the **Second Schedule**. The **Banking Companies Act, 1949** (renamed **Banking Regulation Act in 1966**) gave **statutory direction** to banking business and its **regulation by the Reserve Bank**, including **control over management** and an **override mechanism**.

**Five parts:**

- **Part I:** short title, extent, commencement (also certain **co-operative societies**).
- **Part II:** **forms of business**, constitution and governance, **minimum capital and reserves**, cash reserve, the Reserve Bank's **directions, inspection** and **control over management** (**remove managerial persons, appoint additional directors**, **Government acquisition of undertakings**).
- **Part III:** **suspension of business and winding up** (High Court, **court liquidator**, Reserve Bank as **official liquidator**), **III-A** speedy winding up, **III-B** records and returning paid instruments.
- **Part IV:** **penalties, fines, change of name**.
- **Part V:** application to **co-operative banks**.

**Principal sections (courseware list):** **5 and 6(1)** definitions and forms of business; **8-9** no trade, **non-banking assets** disposed within the **prescribed period**; **10** no **managing agents** or commission-paid staff; **11** minimum **paid-up capital and reserves**; **12** capital proportions and **voting rights**; **13-15** commission, **unpaid capital**, **dividends**; **16** no **common directors**; **17** **reserve fund**; **18** **cash reserve** (non-scheduled banks); **19** **subsidiaries**; **20** no **loans on own shares or to directors**; **21** **directions on advances**; **22** **licensing**; **23** **branches**; **24-25** **liquid assets**; **26** **unclaimed deposits** (**30 days** after the calendar year); **27-28** **returns**; **29-32** **balance sheet, audit**; **35** **inspection**; **36** **caution, prohibition, assistance with amalgamation**, **annual report on Trend and Progress**; **37-45** **moratorium, winding up, amalgamation**; **46-48** **penalties**; **51** **SBI and other notified banks**; **55** amendment of **RBI Act Sections 18 and 42(6)**.

**1950 amendment:** an **amalgamation scheme** needs a **majority in number representing two-thirds in value** of **each bank's shareholders**, then **Reserve Bank sanction**; it also gave the Reserve Bank **licensing power over branches abroad**. The Act repealed **Part XA of the Indian Companies Act 1913**, the **1946 Branches and Inspection** measures and the **1948 Control Ordinance**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Act turned scattered rules into a single law of banking regulation under the Reserve Bank.

items.title: FEMA and the external sector reforms
items.core_explanation_md:
**Rangarajan High-Level Committee on Balance of Payments (1993):** a **market-determined exchange rate within limits**; **current account convertibility**; **shift from debt to non-debt flows**; **strict regulation of external commercial borrowings (short-term debt)**; **discourage volatile NRI flows**; **free outflows tied to inflows** and gradual freedom for others; **end Government intermediation of external assistance**.

**Milestones:** **LERMS** (dual rate) **March 1992**; **unified market rate from March 1993**; **Article VIII of the IMF Articles accepted in August 1994** (current account convertibility); **Sodhani Expert Group** (**November 1994**, report **June 1995**) on the forex market; **Tarapore Committee on Capital Account Convertibility (1997)**, which set **three preconditions**: **fiscal consolidation**, a **mandated inflation target** and **strengthening the financial system**.

**FEMA, 1999 (effective June 2000)** replaced **FERA, 1973**: from **conservation** to **management** of foreign exchange; **genuine current account payments** (except notified items) are released by **authorised dealers** without restriction; **surrender of export proceeds** continues; the RBI controls **capital account transactions**.

**Differences from FERA (Box 5.1):** **civil**, not criminal, treatment: the prosecution **need not prove guilt**; **monetary penalties**; an **Adjudicating Authority, Special Director (Appeals) and Appellate Tribunal**; **compounding**: a contravener may apply, and the **compounding authority must decide within 180 days**; the **Reserve Bank** is the compounding authority for all contraventions **except hawala**, where the **Directorate of Enforcement** is.

**Market development:** wide delegation to **authorised dealers**; **options, cross-currency options, swaps, caps/collars and FRAs**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: FEMA shifted foreign exchange law from prohibition to facilitation, backed by civil penalties and compounding.

self_check.prompt_text: Within how many days must the compounding authority dispose of a FEMA compounding application?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 180 days.

items.title: The Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021: scope, maintainability and procedure
items.core_explanation_md:
**What it is:** a **cost-free redress** mechanism for **deficiency in service** by **regulated entities**, under **Section 35A (BR Act)**, **Section 45L (RBI Act)** and **Section 18 (PSS Act)**. It **integrates** the **Banking Ombudsman Scheme 2006**, the **NBFC Ombudsman Scheme 2018** and the **Ombudsman Scheme for Digital Transactions 2019** (**all repealed**); it also covers **non-scheduled primary co-operative banks with deposits of Rs 50 crore and above**; **One Nation One Ombudsman** (**jurisdiction neutral**).

**Features:** the complainant **need not name the scheme**; **deficiency in service** is the ground with a list of **exclusions**; **no territorial jurisdiction per office**; a **Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre, Chandigarh**; the regulated entity's **Principal Nodal Officer** is a **General Manager** (or equivalent) at **head office**; the **Appellate Authority** is the **Executive Director in charge of the Consumer Education and Protection Department**; an entity **cannot appeal** an Award issued because it **did not give satisfactory information on time**.

**Awards:** no cap on the **amount in dispute**; compensation for **consequential loss up to Rs 20 lakh** plus **up to Rs 1 lakh** for **time, expenses, harassment and mental anguish** (courseware, dated). The Ombudsman is an **RBI officer** appointed for **up to three years**; an **annual report** goes to the **Deputy Governor** as on **31 March**.

**Complaint is not maintainable** for: **commercial judgment** of the entity; **vendor outsourcing disputes**; a grievance **not addressed to the Ombudsman directly**; **general grievances against management**; **action under orders of a statutory or law enforcing authority**; services **outside RBI purview**; disputes **between regulated entities**; **employer-employee disputes**; a remedy under **Section 18 of the CIC Act**; customers not covered.

**A complaint lies only if:** the complainant first **complained in writing to the entity** and the reply was **rejected or unsatisfactory** or **no reply came in 30 days**; the complaint reaches the Ombudsman **within one year** of the reply (or **one year and 30 days** from the complaint if no reply); it is **not pending or decided elsewhere** (Ombudsman, court, tribunal, arbitrator); **not frivolous or abusive**; the first complaint was within **Limitation Act** time; the complainant gives **complete information**; and it is lodged **personally or by an authorised representative who is not an advocate**.

**Procedure:** file **online (cms.rbi.org.in)** or via the **Centralised Centre**; the entity files its **written version within 15 days**; failing which the Ombudsman may pass an **ex-parte order**. **Resolution:** **settlement**, **complainant's agreement** or **withdrawal**. An **Award** **lapses unless accepted in 30 days** and the entity **complies within 30 days of acceptance** unless it appeals. **Appeals:** the **entity** (with **prior sanction of the CMD/CEO or ED**) or the **complainant** within **30 days** (up to **30 more** on cause); the **Appellate Authority** may **dismiss, allow, remand, modify** or pass other orders. Banks must **display** the **Ombudsman's contact details** and the **Scheme**, appoint **Nodal Officers** at regional and zonal offices and a **Principal Nodal Officer**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Scheme gives customers a free, single-window route when a regulated entity does not resolve a complaint.

self_check.prompt_text: Within how many days must a regulated entity reply to a written complaint before the customer can approach the Ombudsman?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Thirty days.

items.title: Financial sector reforms after 1991
items.core_explanation_md:
**Before reform (1980s):** **segmented, controlled markets**, **regulated rates**, **public sector bank dominance with high NPAs**, and **SLR** forcing banks to lend to the Government at **below-market rates**.

**1991 crisis:** high **inflation (peak 17 per cent annualised in August 1991)**, high **fiscal deficit**, low growth, an **unsustainable current account deficit** (Gulf war) and a **balance of payments crisis**. **Response:** **stabilisation**, **deregulation** (end of licence-permit), **liberalisation of trade**, **globalisation**.

**Narasimham Committee on the Financial System (1991-92):** **first phase** (**deregulation**, **new private banks**, **prudential norms**, **capital adequacy**, **payment systems**, **Board for Financial Supervision**, **recapitalisation**, **debt recovery**); **Committee II** led to a **second phase** (**prudential aspects**: **risk weights for government securities** and **forex and gold open positions**, **higher capital adequacy**, the **90 day delinquency norm** for income recognition, **State-guaranteed assets** to be treated as NPA in some cases).

**Debt recovery:** the **Tiwari Committee (1981)** and Narasimham proposed **special tribunals**; the **RDDBFI Act, 1993** created **Debts Recovery Tribunals** and **Appellate Tribunals** (the courseware says **33 DRTs and 5 DRATs**); each DRT has a **Presiding Officer** and **two Recovery Officers**. Banks go to the DRT under the **RDDBFI Act**, while under **SARFAESI (2002)** **borrowers and others aggrieved by a bank action** go to the DRT. The **2016 Amendment Bill** changed the **SARFAESI, RDDBFI, Indian Stamp and Depositories Acts**; **ARCs** are subject to RBI **audit and inspection** and **fit and proper** criteria for sponsors (**Master Circular of 10 February 2022**).

**Other segments:** **DFIs** and **NBFCs** under RBI regulation; **IRDA Act 1999** (insurance opened); **SEBI (1992)**; **UTI** monopoly ended **1992**; **ADRs, GDRs, FCCBs, ECBs**; **FII** access with **full capital convertibility**.

**Debt market reforms:** **September 1994** agreement to phase out **ad hoc Treasury Bills** (**discontinued from 1 April 1997**); **Government Securities Act, 2006** (**in force from 1 December 2007**) **replaced the Public Debt Act, 1944**; **market-related rates** and **auctions since April 1992**; **LAF**: an **interim facility in 1999** (export refinance, **CLF**, **ACLF**, **PD liquidity support**) and **full LAF in stages from June 2000 and May 2001**; **CBLO** (CCIL, **January 2003**) later replaced by **tri-party repo**; **CD minimum maturity cut from 15 to 7 days** (**April 2005**).

**Outcomes (dated):** growth about **6.4 per cent**, inflation about **5 per cent**, fiscal deficit **5.1 per cent of GDP** and reserves **US$ 42.3 billion** (**March 2001**).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The reforms replaced administered controls with prudential norms, market pricing and legal recovery tools.

self_check.prompt_text: Which Act created the Debts Recovery Tribunals?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions (RDDBFI) Act, 1993.

items.title: Other financial regulators and the division of functions
items.core_explanation_md:
**Four approaches to supervision:**

| Approach | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Institutional** | Each **category of institution** has its own supervisor (traditional) |
| **By objectives** | Each authority handles **one objective** (for example **prudential** or **conduct**) across institutions |
| **Functional** | Supervision follows the **economic function**, whatever the institution |
| **Single regulator** | **One authority** for **all markets and intermediaries** (the **UK FSA** model) |

No model is clearly superior; **most countries** keep **bank supervision in the central bank**.

**India (institutional model):** the **Reserve Bank** supervises **banks, NBFCs and all-India financial institutions**; the **Registrar of Co-operatives (State)** is a **joint regulator** of **co-operative banks**; **SEBI** regulates **capital markets** (stock exchanges, mutual funds, brokers, merchant bankers, rating agencies); **IRDA** regulates **insurance**.

**Overlap and coordination:** the **Khan Working Group** argued for a **Super Regulator** and the **Deepak Parekh Group** for **legal status** for the **High Level Coordination Committee on Financial and Capital Markets (HLCC)**, chaired by the **Governor** with the **Finance Secretary** and the **Chairmen of SEBI and IRDA**, with **three Technical Standing Committees** (banking, insurance, capital markets). Other views: the **duality of control** between the Reserve Bank and the **Banking Division, Ministry of Finance** should end; an **apex regulatory authority** chaired by the **Governor** could coordinate. The courseware concludes that **regulatory overlaps and arbitrage are small** and that the Indian model works with **coordination**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: India has several specialised regulators coordinated by a high-level committee rather than a single super regulator.

self_check.prompt_text: Who chairs the High Level Coordination Committee on Financial and Capital Markets?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Governor of the Reserve Bank.

items.title: Institutions set up by the Reserve Bank
items.core_explanation_md:
**Agriculture and rural credit:** the **All-India Rural Credit Survey (Gorwala, 1951)** led to the **Imperial Bank's nationalisation (SBI, 1955)**; the **1955 RBI Act amendment** created the **National Agricultural Credit (Long-Term Operations) and (Stabilisation) Funds**; **Agricultural Refinance Corporation (1963)** became **ARDC** and then **NABARD** (**12 July 1982**): **initial capital Rs 100 crore** (Government and RBI equally); **short-term refinance** (up to **18 months**), **medium term (3-7 years)** and **long term (up to 25 years)**; the **RRBs and co-operatives** now fall under **NABARD supervision**.

**Industry and finance institutions:**

| Institution | Key facts (courseware) |
| --- | --- |
| **IDBI** | **IDBI Act 1964**; set up **1 July 1964** as an **RBI subsidiary**; **de-linked in February 1976**; four roles (**coordinating, financing, refinancing, promotional**); became a **bank** under the **2003 Repeal Act** (**IDBI Ltd incorporated 27 September 2004**; **IDBI Bank Ltd from 7 May 2008**) |
| **DFHI** | **April 1988**, after the **Vaghul Committee**; secondary market for **money market instruments** (T-bills, commercial bills, CDs, CP); **dated securities from April 1992**; **Primary Dealer from 29 February 1996**; now **SBIDFHI** |
| **IRBI** | **IRCI (April 1971)** → **IRBI (1985, IRBI Act 1984)**: **reconstruction and rehabilitation** of **sick industry** |
| **UTI** | **Trust under the UTI Act 1963**, **February 1964**; **RBI associate until 1976**, then IDBI; **bifurcated after 2001**: **UTI Mutual Fund** and **SUUTI** |
| **EXIM Bank** | **1 January 1982**, **Export-Import Bank of India Act 1981**; took over IDBI's **export financing**; **lines of credit** abroad, **Overseas Investment Finance**, **export marketing** |
| **NHB** | **9 July 1988**, **National Housing Bank Act 1987** (Presidential assent **23 December 1987**); **RBI wholly owned**; **Rangarajan group**; apex for **housing finance**; **HFC regulation moved to the RBI** |
| **CCIL** | **April 2001**; clearing and settlement for **money, G-secs and forex**; **NDS live 15 February 2002**; **CBLO January 2003**; **FX-CLEAR 7 August 2003**; **CLS settlement from 6 April 2005**; runs **NDS-OM and NDS-CALL** |
| **BCSBI** | **2006**, a **self-regulatory** society (**Tarapore Committee 2003** recommendation); **dissolved from 28 September 2021** (courseware) |
| **NPCI** | **Incorporated December 2008** (Section 25 company; **commencement April 2009**); **umbrella for retail payments**; **NFS (taken over from IDRBT)**, **IMPS, ACH, EBT, RuPay**, **UPI** (built on IMPS using a **Virtual Payment Address**) |
| **NARCL** | An **ARC** capitalised by banks and FIs; buys NPAs of **Rs 500 crore and above** for **15 per cent cash and 85 per cent security receipts** guaranteed by Government (dated figures not taught); **PSBs and Government-owned FIs hold at least 51 per cent** |
| **NaBFID** | Development finance institution for **infrastructure**, the **fifth AIFI** after **Exim, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI** |

**PCA for NBFCs (Table 5.1):** thresholds for **CRAR (15 per cent regulatory minimum)**, **Tier I (10 per cent)**, **net NPA** and **leverage** (dated table, not taught).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Institution building let the Reserve Bank supply term finance, markets and payments infrastructure.
