items.title: Objectives of financial inclusion and the impediments (IIT)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Three objectives:** **broaden** services to people and firms **with no access**; **deepen** services for those with **minimal access**; and improve **financial literacy and consumer protection** so people **choose appropriately**.

**Why it matters:** it is a policy goal in **over 60 countries**, central to the **UN 2030 SDGs**, supports **stable financial systems** (the **UNCDF** finds the included **ride out interest rate cycles** without being hurt **counter-cyclically**) and **strengthens monetary policy transmission**. In India growth since independence left many outside **formal finance**.

**Impediments (Raghuram Rajan's IIT):**

| Letter | Impediment |
| --- | --- |
| **I - Information** | The excluded work **informally**, keep **no records**, own **little property**: lenders cannot judge **creditworthiness** |
| **I - Incentives** | Lenders avoid them when **repayment cannot be enforced** quickly or cheaply and there is **no collateral** |
| **T - Transaction costs** | **Fixed costs** are high relative to **tiny loan sizes** (the same effort for a **Rs 10,000** loan as for **Rs 10 lakh**) |

Excluded people may also live **remotely** and lack **institutional arrangements** that reward those who serve them.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Rajan's three letters explain why small, informal borrowers are costly for banks to serve.

self_check.prompt_text: What does IIT stand for in Raghuram Rajan's characterisation of the impediments to financial inclusion?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Information, Incentives and Transaction costs.

items.title: Mandates and subventions
items.core_explanation_md:
**Tools:** **priority sector lending targets**, **opening 25 per cent of branches in unbanked areas**, **interest subventions** and drives such as **PMJDY accounts** and **Mudra loans**.

**Case for mandates:** inclusion has **positive externalities** that the provider cannot capture (the **social status** a worker gains from her **poultry farm** may exceed the bank's cost) and **network benefits** (**direct benefit transfers** and **UPI** work better when **nearly everyone has an account**).

**Risks:** **no market test** of usefulness, **vested interests** keep mandates **alive**, banks **target the easiest eligible borrowers** and **mislabel** normal lending, and **public sector banks** bear most of the burden, which **hurts their profitability**.

**RBI refinements:** revised the **priority sector list** to target the **truly excluded**; **large loans to agri-product firms no longer qualify**; targets are met **every quarter** (limiting **window dressing**); **Priority Sector Lending Certificates** let banks **sell over-achievement**; the courseware says **explicit subsidies** are better than **hidden cross-subsidies** (for example **cash recyclers in underserved areas**). **Mandates are not costless**: cost should be **brought into the open**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Mandates work best when targeted and paid for openly.

self_check.prompt_text: What do Priority Sector Lending Certificates allow a bank to do?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Sell over-achievement in a category to banks that are deficient in it.

items.title: Institutions, digital technology, credit information and payments
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why local institutions:** moneylenders succeed through **local knowledge**; **large bank managers** are often **outsiders** and **centralised**; **HDFC Bank** grew in **Kashmir** by hiring **local loan officers**; **MFIs** use **peer pressure and frequent repayment**. **Limits:** MFIs lack **low-cost deposits**; **local area banks** face **geographical concentration**; **RRBs** are costly and **co-operative banks** suffer **governance weaknesses** with **split supervision**.

**Small finance banks:** 'small' refers to the **customer**; **75 per cent of loans to the priority sector** and **50 per cent of the portfolio in loans below Rs 25 lakh**.

**Information tools:** **credit information bureaus** (**CIBIL**, one free report a year); bringing **SHG borrowing** into their ambit; **Aadhaar** for identity; **Udyog Aadhaar** for small firms; **digitised land records** (a **Rajasthan** proposal) to make **land usable as collateral**; **TReDS** platforms let **MSMEs** sell claims on **large buyers** instead of waiting for late payments.

**Payments before credit:** encourage **savings** and let **credit follow** (as **SHGs** do). Easy **cash in and out** needs **banking correspondents** (a **registry**, **Aadhaar Enabled Payment System**, training, pay), **post office and telecom payments banks**, **UPI** (a **mobile number or alias** is enough), and **75 digital banking units** launched on **16 October 2022**. Small businesses can build **verifiable revenue records** on **online platforms**, and **peer-to-peer lending** under **light-touch regulation** may help.

items.title: Issues in financial inclusion and their resolution
items.core_explanation_md:
**Five issues:** **KYC**, **competition and exploitation**, **flexibility and forgiveness**, **skilling and support**, **financial literacy and consumer protection**.

- **KYC:** the Reserve Bank has **eased documentation**: **one document for permanent address**, **self-certified current address**, **basic (small) accounts** with limits; the **Indian Banks' Association** could use **common account forms**.
- **Competition:** exploitation comes from **moneylenders and corrupt bankers**; **competition** is the main protection. **Interest rate ceilings** can backfire (**hidden fees**, or lenders **stop lending**): the Reserve Bank follows the **Goldilocks principle** for micro finance. **Collateral bans** can also **cut access**; a compromise is **collateral-free loans for priority sector status** while letting banks **charge lower rates on secured loans**.
- **Flexibility and forgiveness:** the biggest part of interest cost is the **credit risk margin**; fix the **lending framework** and allow **restructuring of agricultural loans after natural calamities without NPA classification**, **moratoria** during unemployment and **personal bankruptcy** used sparingly.
- **Skilling and support:** access alone does not lift the poor; they need **skills, marketing and money management** (**Jivika** in Bihar, **Skill India**).
- **Literacy and protection:** guard against **aggressive selling and mis-selling**; **Financial Literacy Centres** in all districts (**June 2012**) holding **monthly camps**; the **2015 Charter of Consumer Rights** (five principles); an **internal ombudsman** in banks; the **Integrated Ombudsman Scheme** strengthens redress.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Inclusion needs documentation relief, competition, forgiveness, skills and protection together.

self_check.prompt_text: What principle does the Reserve Bank follow in setting interest rate ceilings for micro finance firms, as described in this unit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Goldilocks principle: neither too high nor too low.

items.title: Progress, business correspondents and the link with monetary policy
items.core_explanation_md:
**JAM trinity:** **Jan Dhan Yojana + Aadhaar + Mobile**, a **game changer** for **direct benefit transfers**; **PMJDY** began in **August 2014** (**97 per cent** of accounts in PSBs and RRBs, women about **55.6 per cent**).

**Strategies and indices:** the **National Strategy for Financial Inclusion 2019-2024** and the **National Strategy for Financial Education 2020-2025**; the **Financial Inclusion Index (August 2021)**: **97 indicators** across **access, usage and quality**, scored **0 to 100**.

**Pillars:** **digital technology (FinTech)** and **women's participation**. **Financial Inclusion Plans** were introduced in **2010** to push banks to a **planned approach**.

**Intermediaries:**

| Model | Allowed entities | Activities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Business Facilitator** | NGOs, farmers' clubs, co-operatives, **post offices**, **insurance agents**, Panchayats, **Krishi Vigyan Kendras** and others | **Identify borrowers**, **process loan applications**, **awareness and counselling**, **promote SHGs/JLGs**, **monitor and follow up** (no RBI approval needed; **not banking business**) |
| **Business Correspondent** | **NGOs/MFIs**, **Section 25 companies**, **NBFCs not taking deposits**, **post offices**, societies | All BF services plus **small credit disbursal**, **recovery**, **small deposits**, **micro insurance/mutual fund/pension sales** and **remittances**; banks need a **Board policy**, **KYC/AML**, **due diligence**, an **annual review** and **grievance redress** |

BCs supply **more than 95 per cent of banking outlets in villages** (**March 2021**).

**Monetary policy link:** inclusion **improves interest-rate transmission**: the excluded keep **cash under the pillow** (not interest-sensitive); as they join, savings shift to **interest-bearing deposits** and **credit** (interest-sensitive) grows, so **policy rate changes reach more people**. **NABARD's SHG-bank linkage** is the **world's largest microfinance programme**; **RBI Kehta Hai** and **IVRS** spread literacy.
items.expanded_explanation_md: More people holding deposits and loans means more households respond to interest rate signals.

self_check.prompt_text: How does financial inclusion strengthen monetary policy transmission?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It moves people from cash to interest-bearing deposits and credit, making more households sensitive to policy rate changes.

items.title: Goals, targets, indicators and the objectives of monetary policy
items.core_explanation_md:
**Meaning:** monetary policy changes the **supply of money** to promote **growth with price stability**. Money is a **liability of the Government and the central bank** and an **asset of the public**, so policy changes **portfolio choices**.

**Typical goals:** **maximum feasible output**, **high growth**, **full employment**, **price stability**, **fairer distribution** and a **healthy balance of payments**.

**The chain:** **Instruments → Indicators → Targets → Goals**. The further from the instrument, the **harder it is to measure** the effect. **Target variables** should be **close to goals**, **quickly influenced by policy** and **observable**: **money supply, bank credit, interest rates**. **Money supply** is preferred because policy factors dominate it. An **indicator** should show the **intensity of policy**: of the four (**high powered money, money supply, bank credit, interest rates**), **high powered (reserve) money** is the better indicator since the **money multiplier is behavioural**. Example: a **CRR change** alters **reserve money**, then **money supply**, then **prices**.

**Tinbergen principle:** **n objectives need at least n instruments**.

**Price stability argument:** it gives investors a **stable climate**, protects **poorer sections**, and avoids **redistribution between creditors and debtors**. **Barro**: **inflation above about 10 per cent hurts growth**, **optimal growth** needs inflation **below about 7 per cent**; a recent study puts the **threshold at 1-3 per cent for industrial** and **7-11 per cent for developing** countries; the courseware reports that **4 per cent (± 2 per cent)** is the **comfort zone** for the Reserve Bank.

**Single inflation target:** **transparent, clear, holds the bank accountable**; given as a **band**. Some countries (**New Zealand, Canada, UK, Australia, Sweden, Finland, Spain**) adopt **price stability as the sole objective**; the **US** follows a **dual mandate**.

**Reconciling dual objectives:** **unemployment data are weak**, so banks estimate **potential output** and try to **minimise the output gap** (actual vs potential output); in developing economies the **trend growth** is used as a proxy.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Targets and indicators let the central bank steer toward the final goals in stages.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Instruments, indicators, targets, goals.

items.title: Rules versus discretion: Friedman rule and the Taylor rule
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why rules:** they **shape expectations and credibility**, **chart a direction**, require **control of the rule variable** and make policy **transparent**.

**Friedman rule:** make **money supply growth equal to output growth** and prices stay stable (inflation zero). **Friedman guess:** about **4 per cent** money growth to allow **3 per cent real growth** and **1 per cent decline in velocity**. **Criticisms:** the bank **cannot directly control money supply** and the money-price link may shift with **payments technology**.

**Taylor rule (John B Taylor):** **R = r* + p + a(y - y*) + b(p - p*)**, where **R** is the **target short-term rate**, **r*** the **equilibrium real rate**, **p** inflation, **p*** target inflation, **y** output and **y*** potential output; **a and b** are **policy weights** (Taylor proposed **a = b = 0.5**).

- A **1 percentage point rise in inflation** calls for a **rise in the nominal rate of more than 1 point** (**1 + b**, so **1.5** with b = 0.5): the **Taylor principle**.
- A **1 per cent fall of GDP below potential** calls for a **0.5 per cent cut**.
- **Limits:** it is **not valid in open economies** with significant exchange rate effects and is **hard to apply in EMEs** (equilibrium real rate, potential output and the target are hard to measure). **No central bank formally adopts it.**

**Case for rules:** discretion can lead to **time inconsistency** (short-run **accommodation** with long-run inflation); **credibility** depends on **commitment**.

**Case for discretion:** **uncertainty** about **policy impact and lags**, **global shocks**, **capital mobility**, **financial sector fragility** and **financial stability** needs. **Conclusion:** **rules** suit routine price stability and **credibility**; **discretion** suits **crises**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Taylor principle requires the real interest rate to rise when inflation rises.

self_check.prompt_text: According to the Taylor rule with b = 0.5, by how much should the nominal rate rise when inflation rises by one percentage point?
self_check.expected_takeaway: By 1.5 percentage points.

items.title: Instruments: Bank Rate, OMO, LAF, CRR, SLR and selective credit control
items.core_explanation_md:
**Indicators watched:** **narrow, broad and reserve money**, **bank credit**, **industrial sales**, **imports**, **consumption**, **fiscal position**, **prices**, **exchange rates**, **NPAs and payment data**.

**Instruments:** **Bank Rate**, **Open Market Operations**, **reserve requirements** and **selective credit control**.

- **Bank Rate:** rate at which commercial banks **borrow or rediscount** from the central bank; lending is **collateralised** with **margins**; indicative, effective with OMOs; in India also used for **refinance**.
- **OMOs:** **buy and sell** government securities (mostly **secondary market**). **Purchase raises** high powered money; **sale reduces** it. In India the effect is **small** because the Reserve Bank has a **captive government securities market**. **Repos**: the bank **sells** securities with a promise to **buy back** (withdraws liquidity); **reverse repos** inject liquidity. Treasury bills of **7, 14, 28, 91, 182, 364 days** suit fine-tuning.
- **LAF (introduced 2000):** **overnight and term repo and reverse repo**, the **SDF** and the **MSF**. **Corridor:** **MSF (ceiling)**, **policy repo rate (middle)**, **SDF (floor)**. **SDF**: **uncollateralised** deposits at **25 basis points below repo** (from **April 2022**, replacing the fixed reverse repo as the floor). **MSF**: **penal** borrowing by dipping into **SLR securities up to 2 per cent**, at **25 basis points above repo**. **Main liquidity tool**: **14-day variable rate term repo/reverse repo** timed with the **CRR cycle**.
- **CRR (Section 42, RBI Act):** **primary reserve** held with the central bank as a **percentage of net demand and time liabilities**; averaged over a **fortnight**; the **3 to 15 per cent** limits were **removed by the 2005 amendment**; **no interest** paid (from **fortnight beginning 31 March 2007**); the daily minimum is **95 per cent**; default penal interest **3 per cent per annum above the Bank Rate**. **Banks hold excess reserves** for **currency drain and clearing drain**.
- **SLR (Section 24, BR Act):** **secondary reserve** in **government and approved securities, balances, gold and call money**; **history:** **20 to 25 per cent (1962)**, **25 to 38.5 per cent (1970-1990)**, **up to 40 per cent power (1983)**, **scaled down to 25 per cent (October 1997)**, **20 per cent (June 2017)**; the **courseware shortcoming**: governments can use SLR to **finance deficits** cheaply. **Penalty:** **3 per cent over the bank rate**, **5 per cent** if it continues.
- **Selective credit control:** **exposure limits**, **directed lending (priority sector)**, **higher margins on commodity inventories**; used **sparingly**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The policy repo rate sits in the middle of a corridor bounded by the SDF and the MSF.

self_check.prompt_text: Which rate is the floor and which is the ceiling of the LAF corridor?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The SDF rate is the floor and the MSF rate is the ceiling.

items.title: Monetary policy transmission mechanisms and channels
items.core_explanation_md:
**Four traditional mechanisms:** (1) **Quantity theory** (money supply changes shift **prices**; Cambridge version; **Keynes** attacked it; **Friedman** revived it); (2) **Real balance effect** (**M/P**: higher real balances make households **wealthier and consume more**); (3) **Interest rate mechanism** (money affects **bond rates**, then **investment**: Keynes); (4) **Credit availability** (**credit rationing**; easier availability raises **autonomous spending** with a multiplier).

**Channels (BIS):**

| Channel | Chain |
| --- | --- |
| **Money aggregate** | **ΔM → ΔY → ΔP**; via reserves: **ΔRM → ΔMS → ΔP** |
| **Interest rate** | **Δr → ΔI → ΔY → ΔP** |
| **Exchange rate** | **r → exchange rate → net exports → ΔY**; needs **capital mobility** and a **flexible rate** |
| **Wealth / asset price** | **ΔMS → equity prices → wealth → consumption → ΔY**; **Tobin's q** = **market value / replacement cost** (**high q** encourages **investment**) |
| **Credit / balance sheet** | **MP → deposits and bank credit → investment → ΔY**; affects **small firms** and **consumer spending** |

**Evaluation:** the best channel depends on the **stage of development**. **EMEs** face **fiscal-monetary unclarity**, **underdeveloped, poorly integrated markets**, **low interest sensitivity**, **reliance on internal finance**, **weak credit information** and **rate rigidities**. Developing countries stress the **money supply channel** (point or range **monetary targets**, as **Germany** did), but **money demand became unstable** (US after **1973**). In EMEs the **asset price** channel needs **developed stock markets**, the **exchange rate** channel needs an **open economy**, and the **credit** channel is attractive if **bank and market finance** respond to **expectations**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Different economies rely on different channels depending on how developed their markets are.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The market value of firms divided by the replacement cost of capital.

items.title: Transparency, lags and the monetary policy process in India
items.core_explanation_md:
**Transparency:** central banks publish **annual, quarterly and monthly reports**, speeches and data; weaker areas include **minutes**, **agendas** and the **relationship with government**; after the **Asian crisis (1997)** the **IMF** issued a **Code of Good Conduct**; the Reserve Bank puts **LAF-type deliberations** in the **public domain**.

**Lags:** **inside lag** (**recognition** and decision) and **outside lag** (**implementation** and impact: **institutional and legal constraints** and uncertainty about **size and nature of action**); the **impact lag** is about **12 to 18 months** in India. **Interest rate smoothing** means changing the rate in **phased steps** (for example **four steps of 25 basis points** for a 100 point change).

**Indian consultative process:** **pre-policy consultations** with **IBA, FIMMDA, FEDAI, PDAI, ASSOCHAM, FIEO and rating agencies** (from **October 2005**), **Resources Management meetings**, the **Technical Advisory Committee**, the **Financial Markets Committee (daily)**, the **Monetary Policy Strategy Group**, the **Governor's press conference**. **Quarterly reviews** began in **2005-06**.

**Monetary Policy Committee (Sections 45ZB-45ZL, RBI Act):** **six members**: **Governor (Chair, ex officio)**, **Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy**, **one RBI officer** nominated by the Central Board and **three external members** appointed by the Central Government for **four years**. It meets **at least four times a year** (**currently six**); **quorum four**; **one vote each**, the **Governor has a casting vote** on a tie; each member **writes a statement** explaining the vote; the **resolution** is published after each meeting and **minutes on the 14th day**; the **Monetary Policy Report** is published **every six months**.

**Flexible inflation targeting:** the **Monetary Policy Framework Agreement of 20 February 2015** set the goal of **below 6 per cent by January 2016** and **4 per cent ± 2 per cent** thereafter (**upper 6, lower 2**); the **May 2016 amendment** put it into the Act; **failure** means inflation stays **above the upper or below the lower level for three consecutive quarters**, after which the Bank **reports to the Central Government** the **reasons**, **remedial actions** and **time to return**. The **operating target** is the **weighted average call rate** aligned with the **policy repo rate**.

**Capital inflows in the 2000s:** the **Market Stabilisation Scheme (2004)** sterilised inflows, with **interest costs borne by the Government**, a model of **fiscal-monetary co-ordination**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The MPC makes monetary policy a collective, transparent and inflation-targeting decision.

items.title: Credit policy: meaning, difference from monetary policy and the practice in India
items.core_explanation_md:
**Credit policy** is the policy of the central bank on **the cost and availability of bank credit** to the sectors of the economy; it is a **sub-theme (adjunct) of monetary policy** with a **two-fold role**: its effect on **investment and growth** and on **money supply** (credit creation adds money).

**Dimensions:** the **quantum**, **sources** (institutional and non-institutional; banks are the main source), **nature of requirements** and **allocation mechanisms**.

**Differences from monetary policy:** money is an **asset of the public but a liability of the Government and the central bank**; **bank credit is an asset of banks and a liability of the public**. In a developing country it is not enough to decide the **total credit**: it must also be **allocated across sectors, regions and groups** (sectoral, regional and equity concerns). Instruments are mostly the **same**; credit policy is administered by the central bank.

**What the Reserve Bank regulates:** the **cost**, the **quantity** and the **purpose** of credit; **productive** needs of **agriculture, trade and industry**, **not speculative** uses.

**In practice:** the bank considers the **market borrowing programme**, **foreign capital flows** and **deposit mobilisation** to set the desired **credit expansion**, which also shows the split between **Government** and **commercial sector**. Credit is then allocated **by activity** (agriculture, manufacturing, trade), **by industry class**, **to priority sectors**, and **by region (rural vs urban)**. The **credit budget** is an **offshoot of the monetary budget**; credit planning also means building **infrastructure and channels** for delivery.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Credit policy decides how much credit exists and where it goes.

self_check.prompt_text: What three aspects of credit does the Reserve Bank seek to regulate?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The cost, the quantity and the purpose of credit.

items.title: Nominal and real credit and the credit allocation mechanism
items.core_explanation_md:
**Nominal credit** is measured at **current prices**; **real credit** at **base-year prices**. In **high inflation**, nominal credit is **much higher** than real credit. The authorities control **nominal credit** (through **reserve money**), not real credit, so they restrain it to avoid a **price rise**; **price neutrality** holds only when **real credit also grows**.

**Allocation follows the Five-Year Plans** (physical planning): the credit needed by sector in a year = **Σ (b × planned output + c × planned investment)**, where **b = bank credit-output coefficient** and **c = bank credit-investment coefficient**; close **co-ordination with the Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog)**.

**Four levels of allocation:**

1. **To Government:** the Government borrows from the market; **SLR** makes **banks, LIC and provident funds** hold **government securities**; the Reserve Bank, as **public debt manager**, **dovetails** the **borrowing programme** with the **monetary budget**; if borrowing exceeds what the **SLR and other institutions can absorb**, the bank can **absorb the excess** (**inflationary**) or **raise the SLR** (**crowds out private credit**).
2. **Inter-industry:** by **industrial classification**, to direct credit to **specific purposes** and **selected industries**, integrated with the **Plans**.
3. **Inter-borrower:** based on **interest rate, amount, purpose, collateral and default risk**, with **socio-economic considerations**.
4. **Sector/region/group:** priority sectors, rural and urban.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Planned sector credit equals output and investment multiplied by their credit coefficients.

self_check.prompt_text: Why do the authorities restrain nominal credit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To avoid pushing nominal credit far above real credit, which would raise the price level.

items.title: Instruments of credit control, margins and credit ceilings
items.core_explanation_md:
**Two types of control:**

- **Quantitative:** **Bank Rate**, **OMOs**, **reserve ratios** and **SLR**: they control **total money and credit creation**.
- **Selective:** **directives**, **limits on advances against pledged commodities**, **higher margins**: they control the **allocation** of credit and **curb speculative use**, mainly for **sensitive commodities**.

**History in India:** first used in **1956** to stop **hoarding of food grains** by raising **margin requirements**. Directives covered **oil seeds, vegetable oils, paddy, rice, gram, pulses, cotton textiles**; **margins were raised in 1990** (oil seeds and vegetable oils, **15 percentage points** in steps) and later **relaxed** as supply improved (wheat margins cut **15 points from 16 April 1990**; margin on loans against **shares and debentures** cut from **75 to 50 per cent from 8 April 1993**).

**Credit ceilings (rationing):** limits on advances against commodities, such as **100 per cent of peak credit** from a base period for **wheat, cotton and kapaas (from December 1989)**, a **15 per cent rise in the ceiling from April 1993**, and **removal of bank-wise ceilings on credit against shares and debentures**.

**Limits:** selective controls only help **hold down the price of sensitive goods** and **supplement** general tools; their role has **declined** with **financial deregulation**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Selective controls steer credit; quantitative controls limit its total.

self_check.prompt_text: In which year did India first use selective credit controls, and for what purpose?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 1956, to check hoarding of food grains by raising margin requirements.

items.title: Credit pricing (PLR to MCLR and external benchmarks) and digital lending guidelines
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why pricing matters:** banks are the **main conduit** for policy transmission in India, so how **lending rates follow the policy rate** is a key concern.

**Evolution of benchmarks:**

| Year | System | Key point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1994** | **Prime Lending Rate (PLR)** disclosure | Rate for the **most creditworthy** borrowers, after **deregulation** |
| **2003** | **Benchmark PLR (BPLR)** | Internal reference rate; **sub-BPLR lending** defeated its purpose; ended **30 June 2010** |
| **July 2010** | **Base Rate** | Lending rate = **base rate + borrower-specific charges**; **cost of funds** could be **average, marginal or blended**, so **opacity** |
| **1 April 2016** | **MCLR** | **Marginal cost of funds, negative carry on CRR, operating costs, tenor premium** with tenor-linked benchmarks (overnight to one year) and a **spread** for **credit risk** |

**Problems with MCLR:** transmission stayed **uneven** across **sectors**, between **deposit and lending rates**, and between **fresh and outstanding loans**; the **spread over the one-year MCLR** varied.

**Study Group (August 2017):** **internal benchmarks (base rate, MCLR) did not deliver effective transmission**; **arbitrariness** weakened the process; it recommended an **external benchmark** and, after examining **13 candidates** (WACR, CBLO, market repo, 14-day repo, G-sec yields, **T-bill**, **CD**, MIBOR, MIFOR, OIS, FBIL CD and T-bill rates, **policy repo rate**), found the **T-bill rate, CD rate and RBI policy repo rate** the best suited.

**Digital lending (circular of 2 September 2022):** applies to **commercial banks, RRBs, small finance and local area banks, co-operative banks and NBFCs (including HFCs)**; **outsourcing to a Lending Service Provider or digital lending app does not reduce the regulated entity's obligations** and the LSP and apps must **follow the guidelines**; it applies to **existing customers taking fresh loans** and **new customers** from the circular date, with a **transition to 30 November 2022** for existing digital loans.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Linking loan rates to an external benchmark makes policy changes reach borrowers faster and more evenly.

self_check.prompt_text: Which internal benchmark system took effect on 1 April 2016?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The marginal cost of funds based lending rate (MCLR).

items.title: Monetary-fiscal relations in India: automatic monetisation and the inflation-growth balance
items.core_explanation_md:
**The link:** **harmonising monetary and fiscal policy** is a **prerequisite** for **growth with stability**. **Barro**: **optimal growth** needs inflation **below about 7 per cent**.

**History:** since **1951** the Government ran **large deficits** that the **RBI financed through ad hoc Treasury Bills** (**3-month** bills **renewed** each time, so financing became **automatic**): **automatic monetisation**. The RBI also **bridged the plan resource gap** by **monetising debt** and keeping **government security yields artificially low**: an **accommodative** policy that caused **inflationary pressure** and **financial repression** and **weakened price stability**. Growth stayed around **3 per cent to the 1980s**, about **5 per cent in 1985**.

**Remedies:** **end of automatic monetisation** and a **statutory ceiling on public debt** through the **FRBM Act**, plus greater **co-ordination** between authorities.

**Good practice:** keep **monetary expansion in line with productive capacity**, direct **credit to productive uses**, and **sterilise surplus capital inflows** with **Market Stabilisation Bonds** under the **Market Stabilisation Scheme**.

**Growth vs inflation:** the **2009-11** period saw **high inflation**, with the **repo rate changed more than ten times in two years**; **Subir Gokarn**'s evidence over decades shows **growth rising while inflation fell**, so there is **no long-term trade-off** (stronger still without agriculture).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Automatic monetisation tied the central bank to financing deficits; the FRBM Act and ending ad hocs freed it.

self_check.prompt_text: What was automatic monetisation of the fiscal deficit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The RBI automatically issuing money against renewed ad hoc Treasury Bills to finance the Government.

items.title: Recent finances of the Centre and States (to 2021-22)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Fiscal stance:** an **infrastructure thrust** (the **National Infrastructure Pipeline** and a **Development Financial Institution** announced in **Union Budget 2021-22**) supports recovery. The Centre chose **gradual consolidation** (a **GFD of 6.8 per cent of GDP in 2021-22**, from **9.4 per cent**, falling to **below 4.5 per cent by 2025-26**), emphasising **capital expenditure** (**2.5 per cent of GDP** vs an average **1.7 per cent** in 2010-20).

**Support to States (2020-21):** the **WMA limit raised by 60 per cent (April 2020)**, extended by **Advisory Committee on WMA to State Governments (2021)**; **overdraft days** increased; looser rules on **withdrawing from the Consolidated Sinking Fund**; **interest-free 50-year loans** for **capital expenditure**; **net market borrowing of up to 4 per cent of GSDP in 2021-22** (more with **power sector reforms**).

**Pandemic package (2020-21):** about **Rs 17.2 lakh crore (9.3 per cent of GDP)**: **PMGKP** (26 March 2020), **Atmanirbhar Bharat 1.0** (liquidity, guarantees for **MSMEs, NBFCs, MFIs, HFCs, DISCOMs**), **2.0** (LTC voucher scheme, capex), **3.0** (housing, **NIIF**, **PLI schemes**). The package **overstates** the fiscal cost because it includes **liquidity measures** (below the line); expenditure rose **Rs 30.4 to 34.5 lakh crore** partly from **bringing food subsidy borrowing on budget** (**FCI loans from NSSF**).

**2021-22:** tax **buoyancy** through **compliance, data analytics, AI** and **faceless assessment**; **disinvestment and asset monetisation** under a new **PSE policy** with **four strategic areas** (atomic energy, space and defence; power, petroleum, coal and minerals; transport and telecom; financial services); heavy **market borrowing** and the **NSSF**.

**States:** GFD-GSDP **3.8 per cent in H1 2020-21 against 2.8 per cent budgeted**; states usually **cut capex by about 0.5 per cent of GDP**; the **17 states** budgeted a **GFD of 3.2 per cent of GSDP in 2021-22** (from **4.1**), through **higher revenue and lower revenue expenditure**; grants slated to rise under **FC-XV**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Counter-cyclical capital spending and state support were the main fiscal responses to the pandemic.

items.title: Recommendations of the Fifteenth Finance Commission
items.core_explanation_md:
**Three areas:** **tax devolution**, **grants** and **fiscal roadmap/rules**.

**Tax devolution:** **FC-11** widened the **shareable base to all Union taxes** (excluding **cesses and surcharges**); **FC-14** sharply raised the **devolution ratio** after the **Planning Commission was abolished** and **plan grants ended**. Growth in cesses and surcharges (**outside the divisible pool**) reduced the benefit. **FC-15** kept the **ratio** (adjusted for **Jammu and Kashmir**) for **stability**. **Horizontal sharing** (among States) has used **equity criteria since FC-8**; **FC-15** moved the **population base from 1971 to 2011**, added a **demographic performance** criterion (**to reward population control**: the **inverse of the 2011 total fertility rate times the 1971 population**) and **brought back the tax effort** criterion (used by FC-10 to FC-12, dropped by FC-13 and FC-14).

**Grants:** a **historically high share of grants**; **local body grants** are the **largest**, then **post-devolution revenue deficit grants**; **sector- and State-specific grants** returned.

**Fiscal rules:** FC-12, 13 and 14 recommended **eliminating revenue deficits** and capping the **fiscal deficit at 3 per cent of GDP**; **FC-12** proposed a **sinking fund** and **guarantee redemption fund** for States; **FC-14** excluded States from **NSSF** operations (from **1 April 2015**). **FC-15** **relaxed targets** after the pandemic: **Union GFD** terminal target **3.5 to 4.5 per cent of GDP by 2025-26**; States' **net borrowing** **4 per cent of GSDP in 2021-22**, **3.5 per cent in 2022-23**, **3 per cent from 2023-24 to 2025-26**, plus **0.5 per cent** incentive borrowing for **power distribution reforms**. The **FRBM Act, 2003** sets targets for **fiscal discipline**.

**Roadmap (dated):** Union GFD from **9.3 to 6.8 per cent of GDP (2021-22 to 2025-26)**, **debt 89.6 per cent peak** and **85.7 per cent by 2025-26**; States' GFD from **6 to 4 per cent of GSDP**, debt **62.9 to 56.6 per cent**; an **inter-departmental group** to review **FRBM**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Devolution, grants and fiscal rules together shape how the Centre and States share and spend resources.

self_check.prompt_text: Which base year for population did FC-15 move to in determining each state share?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 2011, from 1971, with a demographic performance criterion to reward population control.

items.title: Liquidity, system liquidity measures and the evolution of the LAF
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why:** liquidity management is the **operating procedure of monetary policy**. A **policy rate** change first moves the **inter-bank call money rate**, then **longer-term rates**, **loan and deposit rates**.

**Meaning:** **central bank liquidity** = **reserves** the central bank provides to banks. Banks must hold **required reserves (RR)**; if the system has **less than required**, liquidity is in **deficit**; more means **surplus**. A **shortage raises rates**; **excess lowers** them.

**Banking System Liquidity (BSL):**

- **TBBLAF** = total borrowings under **repo, MSF and SLF-MF**;
- **RRD** = **reverse repo deposits**; **NBLAF = TBBLAF − RRD**;
- **AR** = actual reserves; **RR** = required reserves; **ER = AR − RR** (excess reserves);
- **BSL = NBLAF − ER**. **Positive BSL = deficit; negative BSL = surplus.**

**Evolution:** **April 1999 ILAF** (injection against government securities; surplus absorbed at a **fixed rate**; **CLF/ACLF**, export credit refinance and PD support linked to the **Bank Rate**) → **full LAF from June 2000**.

- **Stage 1 (5 June 2000):** **flexible repo rate**; reverse repo **above** the repo rate; non-bank lenders in call money allowed to lend up to **85 per cent** of average daily lending.
- **Stage 2 (8 May 2001):** a **normal facility** at the **Bank Rate** (about **two-thirds**) and a **backstop facility** (about **one-third**) at **200-300 bps above repo**.

**Internal Group on LAF (2003, chaired by D. Anjaneyulu):** daily **7-day repo** and **overnight reverse repo**, a **14-day repo** fortnightly, merging normal and backstop facilities into **one facility at the repo rate**; from **October 2004** **overnight fixed-rate repo (ceiling) and reverse repo (floor)**; the **MSS (April 2004)** absorbed capital inflow liquidity.

**Working Group on Operating Procedure (15 March 2011):** **repo rate as the single policy rate**; **WACR** as **operating target**; **corridor** of **150 bps** (repo + 50, reverse repo repo − 100); **Bank Rate reactivated** with an **Exceptional Standing Facility** up to **1 per cent of NDTL**; liquidity around **±1 per cent of NDTL**; minimum daily reserve **from 70 to 80 per cent of CRR**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The framework moved from an injection facility to a corridor around a single policy rate.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the formula for Banking System Liquidity (BSL)?
self_check.expected_takeaway: BSL = net borrowings under LAF minus excess reserves; a positive value means a deficit.

items.title: Later revisions: Patel Committee (2014) and the Internal Working Group (2019)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Patel Committee (2014):** avoid **reliance on overnight variable rate repos**; **term repos of different tenors** provide the **bulk of liquidity**; **end unlimited accommodation at the fixed repo rate**; **fine-tuning repos/reverse repos** (**overnight to 28 days**); **phase out export credit refinance**.

**Internal Working Group (IWG, constituted 6 June 2019, report 26 September 2019):**

- **Corridor** (not floor) system continues.
- **WACR** remains the **operating target**.
- Desired system liquidity: a **small deficit of about 0.25 to 0.5 per cent of NDTL**; use **variable rate operations** if surplus arises.
- **Day-to-day:** one **overnight variable rate operation** at a rate **close to the repo rate**; **no separate assured liquidity**; **standalone primary dealers** may take part directly; **intra-day fine-tuning** only for **unforeseen shocks**.
- **Durable liquidity:** build-ups beyond **0.25 to 0.5 per cent of NDTL** should be offset by **OMOs, forex swaps** and **longer-term (above 14 days up to one year) variable rate repos and reverse repos**.
- **Corridor edges:** **25 bps** between **repo and reverse repo** and between **repo and MSF** retained; **margins** reviewed (reverse repo margin **nil**); **reserve averaging**: **90 per cent of CRR on a daily basis** retained; the **SDF** to be operationalised early; **communication**: **Money Market Operations** release to show **daily flow and stock impact**, and a **fortnightly durable liquidity assessment**.

**Revised framework in practice:** with **WACR** as the single target the **one-sided liquidity target was removed**; the **daily fixed rate repo and the 14-day term repos were withdrawn**; a **14-day term repo/reverse repo at a variable rate**, timed with the **CRR maintenance cycle**, became the **main liquidity tool** (with **fine-tuning operations**).

**Principles:** deficit or surplus is a **design choice**; **fixed rate operations** when **normal**, **variable rate** for **unanticipated** conditions; **banks should prefer trading among themselves** (borrow in the inter-bank market at no more than the **central bank lending rate** and lend at no less than the **central bank borrowing rate**).

**OMO structure:** **government securities of 1 to 20/30 years** and **Treasury Bills (7, 14, 28, 91, 182, 365 days)**; **repos** inject, **reverse repos** absorb.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The IWG kept the corridor and made a 14-day variable rate operation the main tool.

self_check.prompt_text: Which operation became the main liquidity management tool after the IWG recommendations?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A 14-day term repo/reverse repo at a variable rate, timed with the CRR maintenance cycle.

items.title: Liquidity measures during Covid-19 and the April 2022 SDF
items.core_explanation_md:
**Context:** from **February 2019** the **repo rate was cut by 250 bps cumulatively** (135 bps before and **115 bps off-cycle in March-May 2020** by the MPC); system liquidity turned to **surplus from May 2019** and the Reserve Bank **absorbed large amounts daily**. **Measures targeted four levels:** **system**, **sector**, **institution** and **instrument** liquidity.

**Money market:** **abundant surplus** kept the **overnight rate** near the **reverse repo rate (the bottom of the corridor)**; **TREPS and market repo** traded **below the reverse repo**.

**NBFC/HFC stress:** **IL&FS defaulted on its commercial paper in August 2018** and **DHFL** in **2019**; the Reserve Bank allowed **partial credit enhancement by banks**, counted **government securities as Level-1 HQLA** up to **incremental credit to NBFCs/HFCs**, added OMOs and term repos, widened **ECB eligibility to HFCs** and cut the **ECB infrastructure maturity from 5 to 3 years**.

**Tools:** **Long Term Repo Operations (LTROs)** of **1 and 3 years (February 2020)**; **Targeted LTROs** (**27 March 2020**) with funds used for **investment grade corporate bonds, CP and NCDs**; **TLTRO 2.0 (17 April 2020)** with **at least 50 per cent** in **MFIs and smaller NBFCs**; **special refinance of Rs 65,000 crore** to **NABARD, SIDBI, NHB and EXIM**; **Operation Twist** (buy long, sell short government securities, **December 2019**); **Special Liquidity Facility for Mutual Funds (SLF-MF)** in **March-April 2020**.

**Risk-free curve and transmission:** the call money rate moves first, then **risk-free longer rates**, then **loan and deposit rates**.

**8 April 2022:** the **Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)** at **3.75 per cent** became the **floor** (corridor narrowed from **65 to 50 bps**); it **absorbs liquidity without collateral**, and **use is at banks' discretion**, **available after market hours on all days**; **MSF** at **4.25 per cent** is the **ceiling**. The Reserve Bank **moved away from ultra-accommodation** and raised the **held-to-maturity ceiling to 23 per cent** (from 22 per cent) until **31 March 2023**, with the **19.5 per cent cap restored in phases through FY24**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The pandemic response combined policy rate cuts with targeted liquidity to specific markets and sectors.

self_check.prompt_text: What new facility did the Reserve Bank introduce on 8 April 2022 as the floor of the corridor?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF).

items.title: Objectives, legal framework and the four risks in reserve management
items.core_explanation_md:
**Objectives:** **safety and liquidity** are the **twin objectives**; **return optimisation** is sought **within** those limits. The demand for reserves depends on the **exchange rate regime**, **openness**, the **size of the external sector** and **market depth**.

**Why hold reserves:** they show **comfort in meeting international obligations (import payments)** and give a **cushion against external shocks** and **volatile capital flows**. The **transactions motive** is largely met by a **market-determined exchange rate**, but in **transition** reserves **smooth adjustment** and give **additional comfort**.

**Legal framework:** the **RBI Act, 1934** (**Sections 17(6A), 17(12), 17(12A), 17(13) and 33(6)**) allows investment in **deposits with other central banks and the BIS**, **deposits with commercial banks overseas**, **sovereign or sovereign-guaranteed debt with residual maturity up to 10 years**, and other instruments approved by the **Central Board**. Currency composition and investment policy are set **in consultation with the Government**.

**Risks and controls:**

| Risk | Management |
| --- | --- |
| **Credit** | **Highly rated sovereigns, central banks, supranationals**; deposits with **central banks, the BIS, commercial banks**; **counterparty selection guidelines** and **continuous limit monitoring** |
| **Market** | **Currency, interest rate and gold price** risk; gains and losses booked in the **Currency and Gold Revaluation Account (CGRA)**; **dated securities** valued at **market prices weekly and monthly** with changes going to the **Investment Revaluation Account (IRA)** as a **buffer** |
| **Currency** | Long-term **exposure decisions** reviewed regularly |
| **Interest rate** | **Benchmark duration** and **permitted deviation** |
| **Liquidity** | Portfolio kept **highly liquid** (Treasury securities can be sold in size; **fixed deposits** and **supranational** paper are less liquid); the portion convertible into cash at **short notice** is monitored |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Reserves must be safe and liquid first, with returns a secondary aim.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the twin objectives of foreign exchange reserve management in India?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Safety and liquidity, with return optimisation within that framework.

items.title: Operational risk, transparency, composition and sources of variation
items.core_explanation_md:
**Operational risk controls:** **documented procedures**, **separation of front office and back office**, checks at **deal capture, processing and settlement**, **concurrent audit**, **regular reconciliation**, **internal and external audit**, and **SWIFT** (Alliance Access) with strict **security controls**.

**Transparency:** data are published in **Weekly Statistical Supplements, Monthly Bulletins, Annual Reports** and **press releases**; the Reserve Bank follows the IMF **Special Data Dissemination Standards (SDDS)** template, with **monthly** data on its website, and publishes a **half-yearly report** on reserve management (positions at **end-March and end-September**).

**Composition:** **Foreign Currency Assets (FCA)** (a **multi-currency portfolio** valued in **US dollars**; it **excludes** investment in **IIFC (UK)** bonds, **SDR** holdings and amounts lent under the **SAARC swap**), **gold**, **SDRs** and the **Reserve Tranche Position (RTP)** (the **difference between the IMF's holdings of a member's currency and its quota**). Reserves are **expressed in US dollars**; **FCA movements** come from **purchases and sales of foreign exchange**, **income from deployment**, **external aid receipts** and **revaluation**.

**Sources of variation:** the **current account balance**; the **capital account** (**FDI and portfolio investment**, **banking capital including NRI deposits**, **short-term credit**, **external assistance**, **ECBs**, others); and **valuation changes**. On a **BoP basis** (excluding valuation) reserves rose **USD 4.6 billion in April-June 2022**, but **including a USD 22.7 billion valuation loss** (a stronger US dollar) they **fell USD 18.2 billion**.

**Forward book:** the **net forward asset** of the Reserve Bank in the domestic market was **USD 68.20 billion at end-March 2021**.

**International Investment Position (IIP):** the **stock of external assets and liabilities**; the **net IIP is negative** (about **USD 359.8 billion at end-March 2022**), and the **assets-to-liabilities ratio** was about **71.9 per cent**; **debt liabilities** were about **49.2 per cent** of external liabilities.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Valuation changes can swamp transaction flows in the movement of reserves.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the Reserve Tranche Position?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The difference between the IMF holdings of a country currency and the country IMF-designated quota.

items.title: Adequacy of reserves, gold, deployment of FCA and other aspects
items.core_explanation_md:
**Adequacy indicators (December 2021):** **import cover** fell to **13.1 months** (from **14.6** in September 2021); **short-term debt (original maturity) to reserves** rose from **16.5 to 18.1 per cent**; **volatile capital flows to reserves** rose from **64.1 to 65.0 per cent**. Reserve assets are about **two thirds of India's international financial assets**.

**Variation:** over **2021-22** the rise in **foreign-owned assets in India (USD 65.8 billion)** exceeded the rise in **overseas assets of residents (USD 61.1 billion)**, so **net claims of non-residents rose by USD 4.6 billion**; **exchange rate changes** (the **rupee depreciated about 2 per cent** in the quarter) affect **liabilities valued in US dollars**.

**Gold:** at **end-March 2022** the Reserve Bank held **760.42 tonnes** (**453.52 tonnes abroad** with the **Bank of England and the BIS**, **295.82 tonnes domestic**); the **gold share of reserves** rose from about **5.88 to 7.01 per cent**.

**Deployment of FCA (March 2022):** about **67 per cent in securities**, **26 per cent in deposits with other central banks and the BIS** and **7 per cent in deposits with commercial banks overseas**.

**Other items:** the IMF **Financial Transaction Plan** (purchases and repurchases), **New Arrangements to Borrow (NAB)** (India's commitment doubled from **1 January 2021**) and the **Note Purchase Agreement**; **SAARC swap arrangements** (Bhutan, Maldives, Sri Lanka); the Reserve Bank may invest up to **USD 5 billion** in bonds of the **India Infrastructure Finance Company (UK)**.

**Summing up:** reserves are a **comfort level** and **insulation** from external shocks, meet **precautionary** needs and build **confidence**; the Reserve Bank sold dollars to stabilise the rupee after **February 2022**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Adequacy is judged against imports, short-term debt and volatile flows.

items.title: Why financial markets matter, genesis of the Indian money market and its structure
items.core_explanation_md:
**Importance:** a well-functioning market gives **efficient interest rate signals**, helps **market-based monetary policy instruments**, **mobilises savings**, improves **allocative efficiency**, and **cushions external shocks**.

**Genesis:** the **Chakravarty Committee (1985)** and the **Vaghul Working Group on the Money Market (1987)** led to the **Certificates of Deposit and Commercial Paper (1989)**, **inter-bank participation certificates** and the **Discount and Finance House of India (DFHI, 1988)**; the **Narasimham Committee (1992)** started gradual deregulation after the **1991 crisis**. **Call money rates** were freed **before** deposit and lending rates.

**Structure:** the **money market, Government securities market, foreign exchange market** are regulated by the **Reserve Bank**; the **capital market** by **SEBI**; the **insurance market** by **IRDA**.

**Three triggers for the money and G-sec markets:** (1) **ad hoc Treasury Bills (4.6 per cent coupon from December 1974)** replaced by **Ways and Means Advances (1997)**; (2) **indirect instruments** (**Bank Rate reactivated in April 1997**, auctions, private placements and OMOs from **1998-99**, **LAF in June 2000**); (3) a **legal, institutional, technological and regulatory framework**.

**Money market:** the **fulcrum for balancing short-term funds** (maturity up to **one year**), a **focal point for central bank intervention**, and a way for users to get **efficient prices**. The Reserve Bank is the **key constituent**. The call money market was made a **pure inter-bank market** (including **primary dealers**) in phases from **1999**, **completed by August 2005**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Indian money market grew from a narrow, administered market into a deeper market with several instruments.

self_check.prompt_text: Which two committees laid the groundwork for money market reform in the mid-1980s?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Chakravarty Committee (1985) and the Vaghul Working Group on the Money Market (1987).

items.title: Instruments of the money market: Treasury Bills, repo, CBLO, CP, CD and call money
items.core_explanation_md:
**Treasury Bills:** their role was **weakened** because bills created for **deficit financing** were **held by the Reserve Bank**, the **91-day discount rate stayed at 4.6 per cent from 1974**, and bills were **freely rediscounted**; banks used them for **one- or two-day parking**, causing **volatile balances**.

**Call money:** earlier a narrow market of **banks and two all-India institutions**; rates were controlled by the **Indian Banks' Association (IBA)** after rates hit **25 to 30 per cent**: a **15 per cent ceiling from December 1973**, cut to **8.5 per cent by March 1978**, raised to **10 per cent in April 1980**. Average rates ranged from **4.6 to 9.2 per cent in 2000-01 to 2004-05**. The **term money market (over 14 days)** stayed thin.

**Repo:** a **repurchase agreement**; misuse in the **1980s** (buy-back arrangements with non-banks) led to **rules from 1987-88** (no PSU bond buy-backs, **UTI units ineligible from December 1987**, banks barred from repos with non-bank clients from **April 1988**). **Reforms from 1999:** more participants, **delivery versus payment**, **rollover**, **CCIL** support, repo eligibility for select **non-SGL account holders (23 February 2003)** and **non-scheduled urban co-operative banks (11 May 2005)**.

**CBLO:** launched by **CCIL in January 2003** for **non-bank participants** shut out of call money; **unique to India**.

**Commercial paper (CP):** issued by **well-rated corporates and institutions** under RBI terms; **banks are the major investors**; driven by the gap between **CP rates and banks' PLRs**; **delinking from cash credit limits (October 1997)**, **demat-only (October 2002)** and **lower stamp duty (March 2004)** boosted it.

**Certificates of Deposit (CD):** introduced **1989**; **no strong secondary market** because investors **hold to maturity** for higher rates; **demat form** and **lower lock-in** helped.

**Derivatives:** **interest rate swaps and forward rate agreements (1999)**; from **2005** rupee benchmarks such as **MIFOR** only. **Technical Group on the Money Market (May 2005):** stress **collateralised lending**, **yield curve**, **transparency** and **OTC derivative legality**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The market deepened with new instruments, but secondary trading in CP and CD stayed thin.

self_check.prompt_text: Which instrument, launched by CCIL in January 2003, is described as unique to India?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Collateralised Borrowing and Lending Obligation (CBLO).

items.title: The Government securities market
items.core_explanation_md:
**Role:** the G-sec market is the **overwhelming part of the debt market** and its rates are **benchmarks**. The Reserve Bank trades in **Central Government** securities under **Section 17(8) of the RBI Act**; its **regulatory power** over the market comes from **Section 16 of the Securities Contract (Regulation) Act, 1956** (delegated by the Government).

**Pre-1990s:** a **captive market**: **administered low coupons**, **automatic monetisation** through ad hoc bills and a **statutory SLR** (**20 per cent from 16 March 1949 (Section 24, BR Act)**, **25 per cent from 1962/64**, then **34 per cent (Dec 1978)**, **35 per cent (Oct 1981)**, **38.5 per cent (Sept 1990)**; later lowered, **18 per cent of NDTL at 8 October 2022**).

**Reforms in the 1990s:** **auctions for dated securities (June 1992)** meaning **market related coupons**; **uniform price auction** for the **91-day T-bill**; **private placements** with the Reserve Bank for release when conditions were favourable; a range of T-bills (**14, 91, 182, 364 days**); new bonds: **zero-coupon (January 1994)**, **floating rate (1995-96)**, **capital-indexed (December 1997)**, bonds with **call and put options**.

**Institutions:** **STCI (May 1994)**; **Primary Dealers (March 1996)**; **delivery versus payment (July 1995)**; **liquidity support to gilt mutual funds**; **PD conditional repurchase of T-bills (February 2000)**; the **Negotiated Dealing System (NDS) from 15 February 2002** and **NDS-OM (August 2005)** for **anonymous order matching**; **CCIL** as **counterparty**; **FIMMDA** yield curve (**from October 2000**); the **Government Securities Act, 2006**.

**Investors:** banks (dominant because of **SLR**), co-operatives, insurers, provident funds, mutual funds, PDs, NBFCs. **Consolidation:** reissues to **build large securities** (only **20 of 111** securities were **Rs 15,000 crore or more**). **Maturity profile:** average maturity of issuance rose from **5.7 years (1996)** to **14.1 years (2005)**; **30-year and 40-year** securities followed.

**FPI access (from 1 April 2020):** the **general route**, the **voluntary retention route (VRR)** and the **fully accessible route (FAR)**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Auctions, primary dealers and electronic trading replaced administered pricing and a captive buyer base.

items.title: The foreign exchange market, financial benchmarks and the LIBOR transition
items.core_explanation_md:
**Before 1990:** a **controlled regime** with **surrender of foreign exchange** to the Reserve Bank; **FERA** policy created a big **hawala** market. The Reserve Bank bought **Pound Sterling, US dollar (October 1972), Deutsche Mark (1974), Yen (1974)** and sold only **sterling** (the **intervention currency**) until **February 1993**, when the **US dollar** became the intervention currency. From **October 1975** it stopped quoting spot dollar rates; the rupee was **de-linked from sterling** and tied to a **basket** under a **managed float**; banks began **two-way quotes (1975)**; the **1981 internal control guidelines** applied to forex business.

**Reform committees:** **Rangarajan (1992)**, **Sodhani (1995)**, **Tarapore (1997)**; **FEMA's** preamble stresses **orderly development of the forex market**.

**Exchange rate steps:** **July 1991** two-step **downward adjustment**; **1 March 1992 LERMS** (dual rate: **60 per cent at market rate** and **40 per cent at official rate**); **unification effective 1 March 1993**; from **October 1995** no Reserve Bank buying and selling rate, only a **daily Reference Rate** at **noon** from a few Mumbai banks; **July 1995** Government debt service payment made through the **market**.

**Liberalisation:** banks gained **freedom on position and gap limits**, **FCNR(B)** deposit terms, **derivatives**, **borrowing abroad within limits**; corporates may **hedge exposures**, **cancel and rebook forwards**, use **range forwards** and keep **EEFC** accounts. **CCIL** settles **USD/INR spot and forward trades (from November 2002)**, **tom trades (February 2004)** and **guarantees forward trades from the trade date (1 December 2009)**. The **appropriateness standard** guides **derivative sales**.

**Capital account:** **de facto open** for **individuals and non-financial firms**; the Reserve Bank separates **strategic** from **tactical** capital controls.

**Post reform:** daily turnover grew from about **US$ 16 billion (2005-06)** to **US$ 55 billion (2014-15)**; spreads are narrow; in **August 2013** the rupee fell to a low after **QE-tapering fears** and was stabilised by **forex intervention, tighter liquidity, a special FCNR(B) swap window and import restrictions on gold**.

**Benchmarks:** the **LIBOR manipulation scandal (June 2012)** led to the **Vijay Bhaskar Committee (June 2013)**; **FIMMDA** and **FEDAI** became administrators; **FBIL** was formed in **December 2014** (a **private limited company** with **FIMMDA, FEDAI and IBA**) to **develop and administer benchmarks** (**overnight and term MIBOR, CD and T-bill rates, market repo overnight rate, FC-rupee options volatility index**, and later **G-sec valuation** and the **daily USD/INR reference rate**).

**LIBOR transition:** the Reserve Bank asked firms to prepare **Board-approved plans**, stop **new LIBOR contracts**, add **fallback clauses** and prefer **alternative reference rates**; **LIBOR settings ceased or lost representativeness after 31 December 2021 (non-dollar and some dollar settings)** and **after 30 June 2023 (the remaining dollar settings)**; **MIFOR**, which references LIBOR, was to be replaced by **adjusted and modified MIFOR** from **June 2021**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: India shifted from a controlled exchange rate to a market-determined rate with deep spot and forward markets.

self_check.prompt_text: What does FBIL stand for and what does it do?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Financial Benchmarks India Pvt Ltd; it develops and administers financial benchmarks for money, government securities and foreign exchange markets.

items.title: Why banks are supervised and what supervision does
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why banks:** supervision of banks arises from the **fiduciary responsibility** bankers accept when they take **other people's money for safekeeping**, not from doubts about bankers' ability. The act of **deposit taking** is the usual **trigger for statutory control**. There is also a **macroeconomic** concern: banks have a **central intermediary role** and a **sound banking system** is essential to national and international economies.

**Style:** supervision has grown in advanced economies **voluntarily and out of the market**; the supervisor must avoid both **prudential laxity** and **overbearing regulation** ('Scylla and Charybdis').

**UK growth:** after the **secondary banking crisis**, the Bank of England's supervision **widened to institutions not previously under its control** and **stretched across regions and countries**; the **Banking Act 1979** gave it **statutory responsibility** for supervising **deposit-taking institutions** (the courseware also links the formal role to the **Banking Act 1976**).

**International dimension:** banks beyond national borders require **co-operation between supervisors**.

**CAMEL(S):** supervisors examine **Capital adequacy, Management quality, Earnings and Liquidity** (the **missing item is Asset quality**, since **most bank losses arise from lending**).

**Supervisor vs auditor:** the **auditor reports to shareholders** on the **truth of the accounts**; the **supervisor's primary responsibility is to depositors**, so the supervisor must **form his own judgement** and take **action to protect depositors**, looking at **future viability**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Supervisors protect depositors and system stability, which goes beyond the auditor role.

self_check.prompt_text: To whom is the supervisor primarily responsible, in contrast with the auditor?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The bank's depositors (the auditor reports to shareholders).

items.title: Global backdrop: the UK, the US, the Great Depression and Canada
items.core_explanation_md:
**Central banks and stability:** even with narrow mandates, central banks act as **lender of last resort** and manage **interbank liquidity**, so they are **key crisis managers**; but **supervision is not always placed in the central bank**: from the **late 1990s** some countries moved it to **cross-sector authorities**.

**United Kingdom:** no formal banking regulation until the **1970s** except the **Companies Act**; **joint stock banks were allowed from 1826** after repeated failures; **1866 Overend Gurney** and **1878 City of Glasgow Bank** failures; **1890 Baring Brothers**: the **Bank of England** organised a **guarantee fund of over GBP 17 million** to avert crisis, showing its **responsibility for stability**; the **secondary banking crisis (from 1973)** led to a Bank of England **rescue with the clearing banks** and the **Banking Act, 1976**, which raised its **formal supervisory role**.

**United States:** only **State governments** chartered banks until **1863**; the **National Bank Act 1864** created the **Office of the Comptroller of the Currency** to **license banks**; there was **no central bank from 1836 to 1914**; the **Federal Reserve Act 1913 (Owen-Glass)** created the Federal Reserve as a **reserve holder and money-creator of last resort**.

**Great Depression:** by **1933** faith in banks had collapsed; **President Roosevelt** declared a **four-day bank holiday** and the **Emergency Banking Relief Act (9 March 1933)** followed; the **Banking Act 1933** tightened Federal Reserve control and set up the **Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation** to insure deposits **up to US$ 5,000**.

**Canada:** the **Inspector General of Banks (1925)** was created after the **Home Bank** collapse, **nine years before the Bank of Canada (1934)**. **Chile, Mexico, Peru and Scandinavia** developed **central banks and regulators separately**; the **UK and Australia** later **moved regulation to a separate agency**. Structures vary widely but all aim at **systemic stability**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Crises, not design, drove most national regulatory structures.

self_check.prompt_text: Which US Act of 1864 gave the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency the power to license banks?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The National Bank Act of 1864.

items.title: Monetary policy and supervision: benefits, conflicts and integration versus separation
items.core_explanation_md:
**Benefits of integration:** supervision gives the central bank **information** about the **macroeconomy**, **monetary policy options**, **interactions with supervisory policies** and **its own balance sheet**; the value is **greatest in turbulent times**. Supervisory data and **early-warning tools** reveal **credit developments** and show where **monetary transmission is impaired** by weak banks (funding fragilities, NPAs).

**Possible conflicts of interest:** a central bank that supervises banks and also **provides liquidity** may **relax monetary policy** (**inflationary bias**) or **lend to weak banks** (**moral hazard**) for fear that **closing them would cause losses**; in **stress**, **raising interest rates** to fight inflation can threaten **banks' asset values**; managing a **banking crisis** can **divert** attention. (**Stefan Gerlach**).

**Resolution:** research suggests monetary policy should focus on **price stability** and prudential policy on **financial stability**; with **separate objectives and instruments**, a **single institution** can use the **interdependence**; the **European Commission** proposed a governance structure that **strictly separates** monetary and supervisory **decision-making bodies**, with **distinct objectives and instruments**.

**Integration vs separation:** about **three-quarters of OECD countries** give central banks **sole or shared supervision**; the **Bank of England** was **relieved of supervision in mid-1997** when given greater independence; the **Fed** (Greenspan, Bernanke) argues it **needs supervision** to manage crises, ensure payments safety and conduct monetary policy; **Goodhart:** supervisors and central bank staff on systemic stability must **work closely together wherever the supervisors sit**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The debate weighs information gains against the risk of lenient monetary or prudential policy.

self_check.prompt_text: What risk does Stefan Gerlach identify when a central bank with access to liquidity also supervises banks?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It may relax monetary policy (inflationary bias) and encourage bank risk-taking (moral hazard), including lending to weak banks.

items.title: Genesis of bank regulation and supervision in India and the Indian perspective
items.core_explanation_md:
**Early banking (Box 13.1):** the **East India Company** set up the **Bank of Bombay (1720)**; **Warren Hastings** floated the **General Bank of Bengal and Bihar (1773)**; the **General Bank of India (1786)**. The **Presidency Banks**: **Bank of Calcutta (1806)** → **Bank of Bengal (1809)**, **Bank of Bombay (1840)**, **Bank of Madras (1843)**; the **Paper Currency Act, 1861** ended their note issue; the **Presidency Banks Act 1876** put them under one law; the **Imperial Bank of India (1921)** merged them; after the **All India Rural Credit Survey** the **SBI Act (May 1955)** created the **State Bank of India (1 July 1955)**; the **1959 Subsidiary Banks Act** added associates, and the **associate banks and Bharatiya Mahila Bank merged with SBI from 1 April 2017**.

**Early law:** banking was governed by the **Companies Acts** (**1850**, **1857**, **1913**); **limited liability** for banks came later. The **1913 crisis** exposed **low cash ratios** and **large unsecured advances to directors**; the **Indian Central Banking Enquiry Committee (1929-31)** urged a **special Bank Act**; interim measures were the **Banking Companies (Inspection) Ordinance and (Restriction of Branches) Act, 1946**; the **Banking Companies Act, 1949** (later the **Banking Regulation Act, 1966**) followed; the **Department of Banking Operations** of the Reserve Bank (organised **August 1945**) administered it.

**Monetary policy and supervision in India:** financial stability is intertwined with **macroeconomic stability**; **banking distress and currency crises are linked**; banks are the **main vehicle of monetary policy signals**. Supervision gives the Reserve Bank **information** on how its policy affects banks and helps **calibrated tools**. Example: in **December 2004** the **risk weight on housing loans rose from 50 to 75 per cent** and on **consumer credit from 100 to 125 per cent**; in **July 2005** capital market and commercial real estate exposures rose **from 100 to 125 per cent**. The courseware concludes that in India monetary policy and supervision are **complementary rather than conflicting**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Banking legislation in India followed crises and the work of expert committees.

items.title: Development and supervision of commercial banks: 1950 to 1991
items.core_explanation_md:
**Initial years (1950-1969):** many banks failed before 1950; the Reserve Bank's inspection powers began in **1940**, widened by the **Banking Companies (Inspection) Ordinance, 1946** (no prior consent of the bank needed); the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** requires the Reserve Bank, **before granting a licence**, to be satisfied that the company can **pay depositors in full**. Inspection shifted from a **quantitative check of paid-up capital and reserves** to a **qualitative appraisal of financial position, management and methods**; **systematic periodical inspections of all banks started in March 1950**. The **Act was amended in January 1957** (including **refinance** provisions). After the **Palai Central Bank and Laxmi Commercial Bank** collapse (**1960**), the Reserve Bank gained powers for **amalgamation** and **speedy de-licensing**, strengthened inspection (**1961**), looked at **capital adequacy norms** and began **deposit insurance**. The 1960-68 thrust: **soundness**, **consolidation**, **protection of small depositors** (compulsory amalgamations and liquidations), **correcting lopsided branch distribution** by **branch licensing**, and **social control (1967)** over credit deployment.

**Nationalisation and consolidation (1969-91):** **14 banks nationalised on 19 July 1969**; boards constituted on **18 July 1970**; the **National Credit Council** and the **Lead Bank Scheme (December 1969)**; a **branch expansion plan for 1972-74**; **Annual Appraisal** inspection added in **1977-78**; **6 more banks nationalised in 1980**; the target of **40 per cent priority sector advances by 1985**; the **Annual Financial Review from January 1985**; a **Working Group on inspection (December 1981)**.

**1990s reforms:** efficiency and profitability had fallen (directed credit, over-staffing, weak technology), so the **Narasimham Committee (1991)** led to **interest rate deregulation**, **lower CRR and SLR**, **operational autonomy** and prudential norms; **guidelines for entry of private banks in 1993**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Supervision moved from checking solvency to appraising management and operations.

self_check.expected_takeaway: July 1949 (inspections began in March 1950).

items.title: Prudential indicators, supervisory returns and risk management in banks
items.core_explanation_md:
**Supervisory tools:** the Reserve Bank follows **Basel principles**: **capital adequacy**, **asset classification**, **income recognition**, **market valuation of assets** and **recovery of NPAs**, using **on-site** and **off-site** supervision. **Micro-prudential indicators** by **CAMELS** category (**capital ratio; sectoral concentration, foreign currency lending, NPAs, connected lending; expense ratios; ROA and ROE; loan-to-deposit ratio and inter-bank rate spreads; risk management and audit systems; foreign exchange, interest rate, equity and commodity price sensitivity; market-based indicators**) aggregate into the **AMPI**; they are combined with **macroeconomic indicators** and **stress tests** to form **macro-prudential indicators**.

**Returns:** **1999 ALM guidelines** introduced the **Statement of Structural Liquidity** (fortnightly: **domestic, foreign, combined Indian operations, overseas, consolidated**) and **interest rate sensitivity** (earnings perspective by **Traditional Gap Analysis, TGA**). **November 2012** revisions aligned with **Basel III**: **Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)** and **Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR)** returns (**BLR 1 to 5**), and **Duration Gap Analysis (DGA)** (modified duration gap, by currency, monthly) **in addition to** TGA.

**Risk management (October 1999 guidelines):** **four risks** (**market, credit, legal, operational**) plus **systemic risk**; the **Board** sets risk parameters; implementation by a **Risk Management Committee**; a high-level **Credit Policy Committee (CPC)** and an independent **Credit Risk Management Department**; the **ALCO** and CPC integrate credit and market risk. **Credit risk** tools: Board-approved **loan policy**, **delegation of powers**, exposure limits (**single borrower, group, industry, region, sector**), **rating systems**, **loan review mechanism** and **rigorous evaluation of off-balance sheet and inter-bank/country exposures**. **Market risk** tools: **duration, EaR, VaR, simulation, RAROC**. **Interest rate risk:** **gap limits**, **VaR/duration/simulation** and **stress tests**; **currency risk**: **gap limits** with RBI approval and **VaR on forwards**; **operational risk**: proper **measurement and control systems**.

**Regulatory approaches to market risk:** **building block (BBA, as in the 1988 Basel market risk standards)**, **internal models (IMA)** and **pre-commitment (PCA)**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Banks control risk through board policy, limits, committees and independent measurement.

self_check.prompt_text: What additional return and what analysis were introduced for interest rate risk by the revised 2012 guidelines?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Duration gap analysis (and LCR/NSFR returns for liquidity), alongside the traditional gap analysis.
