items.title: Regulatory policies and supervision of scheduled commercial banks (2020-22), the PCA framework and PSB mergers
items.core_explanation_md:
**Covid-19 relief (temporary):** **Resolution Framework (6 August 2020)** to restructure **eligible corporate and personal loans without an ownership change and without downgrading to NPA** (borrowers **standard and not over 30 days past due on 1 March 2020**; invoked by **31 December 2020**; implemented within **90 days (personal)** or **180 days (others)**), guided by the **Kamath Committee**'s **five financial parameters and sector thresholds**; **Resolution Framework 2.0 (5 May 2021)** for **individuals and small businesses** (**aggregate exposure up to Rs 50 crore**). **Ex-gratia** payment of the **difference between compound and simple interest** on loans **up to Rs 2 crore** for the **moratorium period (1 March to 31 August 2020)**. **Gold loans for non-agricultural uses: LTV raised from 75 to 90 per cent**. **Dividend** not to be paid from **2019-20 profits**. **CRR cut to 3 per cent (28 March 2020)** and **restored to 3.5 and 4 per cent** in 2021; **CRR exemption** for **new MSME credit up to Rs 25 lakh per borrower**; **HTM ceiling raised to 22 per cent** (till **31 March 2023**, **restored to 19.5 per cent in stages**); **MSF** dip into SLR **raised to 3 per cent of NDTL** (normal **2 per cent** restored from **1 January 2022**); **last 0.625 per cent of the CCB** and the **NSFR** deferred to **1 October 2021**; the **regulatory retail portfolio limit raised from Rs 5 crore to Rs 7.5 crore** (risk weight **75 per cent**); **LTV-linked risk weights** for **new housing loans (16 October 2020 to 31 March 2022)**; rules on **opening current accounts and CC/OD** tightened from **August 2021**.

**Supervision:** the **Board for Financial Supervision (November 1994)** supervises **SCBs, AIFIs, co-operative banks and NBFCs**; **April 2021 guidelines on appointing statutory auditors** (**independence, conflict of interest**, first extended to **UCBs and NBFCs**).

**Revised Prompt Corrective Action framework (from 1 January 2022):** **timely supervisory intervention** and **market discipline**; key areas **capital (CRAR/CET1), asset quality (net NPA) and leverage (Tier I leverage ratio)**; **negative ROA is no longer a trigger**; PCA is generally based on **audited annual results and supervisory assessment** and applies to **foreign banks' branches and subsidiaries**; **exit** requires **no breach for four continuous quarters (including an audited annual statement)** plus **supervisory comfort**; **mandatory actions**: **restrictions on dividends/remittance of profits and on branch expansion**, **promoter or parent to bring capital**, and **limits on capital expenditure** other than technology. **Lakshmi Vilas Bank** (under PCA) merged with **DBS Bank on 27 November 2020**; **IDBI Bank, UCO Bank and Indian Overseas Bank** exited (2021); only **Central Bank of India** remained under PCA.

**PSB mergers (1 April 2020):** **ten banks into four**: **PNB** (Oriental Bank of Commerce, United Bank of India), **Canara Bank** (Syndicate Bank), **Union Bank of India** (Corporation Bank, Andhra Bank), **Indian Bank** (Allahabad Bank); customers became customers of the **anchor bank**; benefits: **bigger capital base**, **scale**, **efficiency**, **larger customer base**, **global competitiveness**; banks were to appoint **specialised Chief Risk Officers**.

items.title: Recent performance, soundness indicators and developments in the banking sector (2020-22)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Overall (2020-21):** better **asset quality, capital buffers and profitability** despite the pandemic; **credit offtake weak**, **deposit growth strongest in seven years** (led by **CASA**); **credit-deposit ratio down**, **investment-deposit ratio up**; **government securities** preferred; **PSB share in advances and deposits falling since 2010-11**.

**Soundness:** **CRAR rose every quarter to 16.6 per cent (September 2021)**; banks breaching the **10.875 per cent** minimum (including the CCB) fell; **leverage ratio** minimums **4 per cent (D-SIBs) and 3.5 per cent (others)** (earlier **4.5**); **LCR** (30 day stressed outflows covered by **HQLAs**) requirement was **cut from 100 to 80 per cent in April 2020** and restored by **1 April 2021** while banks held **above 100 per cent**; **GNPA ratio 7.3 per cent (March 2021) and 6.9 per cent (September 2021)** via **lower slippages and write-offs**; **Restructured Standard Advances rose** (0.4 to 1.8 per cent); the number of banks under **PCA fell from four to one**.

**Recoveries and ARCs:** recoveries through **Lok Adalats** fell; **fresh IBC proceedings were suspended for a year to March 2021**; the Reserve Bank **disincentivised banks from holding security receipts above 10 per cent of the sale value**.

**Other themes:** **priority sector lending** met targets; **ownership** (PSB mergers, **Lakshmi Vilas Bank into DBS**, **21 PVBs**); **corporate governance** (**Audit, Risk Management and Nomination and Remuneration committees**; **executive pay: variable pay 50-75 per cent of total, at least 60 per cent of it deferred, cash part 33-50 per cent**); **payments** (**RTGS and NEFT 24x7**, **UPI** leads in volume, **Payment Infrastructure Development Fund (January 2021)**, **Digital Payments Index** with **five parameters**); **consumer protection** (**RB-Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 11 November 2021**; **DICGC cover Rs 5 lakh**); **financial inclusion** (**PMJDY, business correspondents, SHG-BLP, TReDS**).

**RBI pandemic response:** **repo cuts of 115 bps in two phases (250 bps cumulative from February 2019)**, **CRR cut of one percentage point**, expanded **MSF**, **LTROs and TLTROs**, **SLF-MF**, **refinance to AIFIs**, **regulatory forbearance** and **digital initiatives** (consumer awareness campaign **RBI Kehta Hai**).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Strong capital and liquidity let banks absorb the pandemic shock, with asset quality improving.

self_check.expected_takeaway: 16.6 per cent against a minimum of 10.875 per cent including the capital conservation buffer.

items.title: Growth of the co-operative credit system and the duality of control
items.core_explanation_md:
**Rural credit institutions:** the **RBI Act 1935** created an **Agricultural Credit Department** (**Section 54**); **Section 17** lets the Bank lend to **state co-operative banks**. After the **All-India Rural Credit Survey (1954)** the Bank set up the **Agricultural Refinance Corporation (1963)** → **ARDC (1975)** → **NABARD (12 July 1982)**, which took over the refinancing functions for **co-operatives and RRBs**; **Regional Rural Banks (1975)** were created because **co-operatives lacked resources**.

**Structure:** a **three-tier rural co-operative structure**: **Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS)**, **District Central Co-operative Banks (DCCBs)**, **State Co-operative Banks (StCBs)**; plus **RRBs, LABs, UCBs** and **commercial bank branches**; about **1,10,000** co-operative institutions. The **share of co-operatives in agricultural credit has fallen** while **commercial banks and RRBs** rose.

**Dual control:** the **State Government and the Registrar of Co-operative Societies** regulate societies working only within the State; the **Banking Laws (Applicable to Co-operative Societies) Act, 1966** (in force from **1 March 1966**) brought **UCBs** under the **Reserve Bank's regulation and supervision**; its powers over **rural co-operative banks** were **limited** and the Act **does not apply to PACS**. Dual control is **contentious**: the **Capoor Task Force (1999)** urged **removal of overlap** and **functional autonomy**, an **Action Plan** and **Memoranda of Understanding** (from **2003-04**); the **Vaidyanathan Task Force (August 2004)** examined the regulatory framework for **rural co-operative banks**, and its recommendations were **accepted in principle**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Overlap between state and central regulators is the structural weakness of co-operative banking.

self_check.prompt_text: Under which Act were urban co-operative banks brought under Reserve Bank regulation, and from when?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Banking Laws (Applicable to Co-operative Societies) Act, 1966, from 1 March 1966.

items.title: Strengthening UCBs and the supervisory system; the 2020 amendment and amalgamation
items.core_explanation_md:
**Prudential norms for UCBs (from 31 March 1993):** **capital adequacy**, an **ALM framework**, more **SLR holdings in government securities**, **limits on loans against shares and debentures** and on **capital market exposure**. The **Madhava Rao High-Power Committee (1999)** reviewed UCBs.

**Supervision:** after the **Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank failure** the Reserve Bank extended **off-site surveillance** to **non-scheduled UCBs with deposits of Rs 100 crore or more**; **supervisory reporting for scheduled UCBs from March 2001**; **capital adequacy phased in from March 2002**; **KYC**; a **ban on loans to directors, their relatives and related concerns from October 2003**; **due diligence on non-SLR investments**; **grading of UCBs from April 2003** (based on **CRAR, net NPAs, losses and compliance**); **CAMELS supervisory rating** (simplified version for **non-scheduled UCBs from March 2004**). The **Draft Vision Document (2005)** sought to rationalise supervision and address **dual control**.

**BR Act amendment 2020:** it improves **governance and oversight** and gives **better access to capital**; effective **29 June 2020** (UCBs, retrospective) and **1 April 2021** (StCBs and DCCBs). **Section 3** exempts **PACS** and societies providing **long-term agricultural finance** (provided they do **not use 'bank', 'banker' or 'banking'** or act as **drawee of cheques**); **Section 45** lets the Reserve Bank **reconstruct or amalgamate** (with or without moratorium) with **Central Government approval**; the Reserve Bank may **supersede the board** (in consultation with the **State Government**); **Section 56** narrows **regulatory arbitrage** with commercial banks.

**Amalgamation:** the **Master Direction of 23 March 2021** (under **Section 44A read with Section 56**) lets UCBs merge voluntarily with **approval of two-thirds of board members**; the Reserve Bank checks whether the merged bank **protects deposits** from **own resources or State support**; incentives include **closing loss-making branches**, **opening branches** and **retaining the AD-I licence**; **24 May 2021** conditions for **DCCB-StCB** mergers.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 2020 amendment gave the Reserve Bank commercial-bank-style tools over co-operative banks.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Approval of the proposal by two-thirds of the board members of the concerned UCB (plus Reserve Bank sanction).

items.title: Recent developments, the umbrella organisation and the four-tier framework for UCBs
items.core_explanation_md:
**2020-21 goals:** refine the **regulatory framework**, a paper on **capital adequacy in UCBs**, a **Supervisory Action Framework (SAF)** for **StCBs and DCCBs** (**NABARD is their supervisor**), and faster resolution of **weak UCBs under All-Inclusive Directions (AID)**. Consolidation is hindered because UCBs are **community or region based**; an **expert committee** (February 2021) studied it.

**Other measures:** **system-based asset classification** (UCBs with assets of **Rs 2,000 crore or more**: from **30 June 2021**; **Rs 1,000-2,000 crore and Level III/IV in cyber security self-assessment**: from **30 September 2021**); **all co-operative banks eligible** for the MSME **Interest Subvention Scheme 2018** (from **3 March 2020**); **ban on director-related loans** (**5 February 2021**); the **umbrella organisation (UO)** for UCBs, **National Urban Co-operative Finance and Development Corporation Ltd (incorporated 18 April 2020)**, to be an **NBFC**.

**Four-tier framework (released 19 July 2022; notified 1 December 2022):**

| Tier | UCBs |
| --- | --- |
| **Tier 1** | **All unit UCBs and salary earners' UCBs**, and others with **deposits up to Rs 100 crore** |
| **Tier 2** | Deposits **above Rs 100 crore up to Rs 1,000 crore** |
| **Tier 3** | **Above Rs 1,000 crore up to Rs 10,000 crore** |
| **Tier 4** | **Above Rs 10,000 crore** |

Deposits are measured on the **audited balance sheet of 31 March** of the previous year; a bank moving up a tier gets a **glide path of up to three years**.

**Net worth:** **Rs 2 crore** for **Tier 1 UCBs in a single district**, **Rs 5 crore** for all others; shortfalls to reach **50 per cent by 31 March 2026** and **full by 31 March 2028**.

**CRAR:** **9 per cent** for **Tier 1**, **12 per cent** for **Tiers 2 to 4** (glide: **10 per cent by March 2024, 11 per cent by March 2025, 12 per cent by March 2026**).

**Financially Sound and Well Managed (FSWM) criteria:** (a) **CRAR at least 1 percentage point above the applicable minimum**; (b) **net NPA not above 3 per cent**; (c) **net profit in at least three of the preceding four years** and **no net loss in the last year**; (d) **no CRR/SLR default** in the previous year; (e) **sound internal control with at least two professional directors**; (f) **Core Banking Solution fully implemented**; (g) **no monetary penalty in the last two years**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Tiering matches regulatory demands to the size and complexity of each co-operative bank.

self_check.prompt_text: What minimum CRAR applies to Tier 2 to Tier 4 UCBs under the revised framework?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 12 per cent of risk weighted assets.

items.title: Financial stability, the 2008 crisis and the post-crisis framework
items.core_explanation_md:
**Cause:** the 2008 crisis grew from **subprime mortgages, mortgage-backed securities and credit default swaps**; **Lehman Brothers** failed on **15 September 2008**.

**Lesson:** **price stability alone does not ensure financial stability**, so central banks added financial stability as an objective with **regulation, supervision, payment systems and monetary policy**.

**New bodies:** **FSOC** (US, Dodd-Frank), the **ESRB** (EU) and the **FSDC** (India).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The unit treats financial stability as a state in which institutions, markets and infrastructure keep working through shocks. The RBI responded to the crisis with liquidity and rate measures. The post-crisis institutional change moved supervisors toward macro-prudential oversight.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is price stability not enough for financial stability?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Severe financial instability can arise even when prices are stable, as the 2008 crisis showed.

items.title: Risks, early warning signals and liquidity principles
items.core_explanation_md:
**Risks:** **herd behaviour**, **payment system failure** and **asset price collapse**.

**Early warning:** indicators of impending crisis, such as the **KLR signals approach**; the RBI publishes the **Financial Stability Report**.

**Liquidity:** the **14 Basel principles** require **senior management involvement** in executing the liquidity strategy; limits on liquid assets against short-term liabilities need a **discount for price volatility**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Early warning indicators are a macro-prudential tool: they flag vulnerabilities before a crisis occurs. Liquidity principles apply to every bank regardless of size.

self_check.prompt_text: Who must be involved in executing the liquidity strategy under the Basel principles?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Members of senior management, on an ongoing basis.

items.title: Supervision machinery and the Basel framework
items.core_explanation_md:
**BFS (November 1994):** Governor as Chairman, Deputy Governor and **four** Directors of the Central Board.

**Ratings:** **CAMELS** for banks, **CALCS** for foreign banks; **OSMOS** started in **1995**.

**Tools:** risk based supervision, **PCA**, **CIBIL (2000)**, DRTs.

**Basel:** the committee began after the Herstatt failure; **three pillars**: minimum capital, supervisory review, market discipline.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The BFS gives supervision a dedicated board separate from monetary policy. Off-site monitoring complements on-site inspection by using returns filed by banks.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the three pillars of the New Basel Accord.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Minimum capital requirements, supervisory review and market discipline.

items.title: Basel II and III implementation in India
items.core_explanation_md:
**Basel II:** parallel run from **1 April 2006**; **standardised approach** (credit), **basic indicator** (operational), **standardised duration** (market); foreign banks and those with overseas presence by **31 March 2008** and others by **31 March 2009**; **Tier 1 six per cent** by 31 March 2010.

**Basel III:** from **1 April 2013**; **common equity 2% → 4.5%**, **Tier 1 4% → 6%**, **2.5% conservation buffer** takes total capital **8% → 10.5%**; adds leverage ratio, countercyclical buffer, **LCR** (from **1 January 2015**) and **NSFR**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The five challenges named are capital, liquidity, technology, skill development and governance. For SIFIs the BCBS planned indicators, extra loss absorbency and enhanced supervision; the FSB set compensation principles with deferral and claw-back.

self_check.prompt_text: By how much does the capital conservation buffer lift total capital?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 2.5 percentage points, from 8 to 10.5 per cent.

items.title: Liberalisation, transparency, and international standards
items.core_explanation_md:
**Monetary policy:** the **multiple indicator approach** from **1998-99**; **fixed rate repo** (December 1997) and **LAF** (June 2000), with repo as floor and Bank Rate as ceiling.

**Market infrastructure:** DvP, CCIL, RTGS, CFMS, NDS; **FMC** reviews conditions daily; **FMD** conducts surveillance.

**Standards:** **SDDS/GDDS** (IMF), **FSF/G-20 (1999)**, **FATF (1989)** with **40 recommendations**, **ROSCs** report compliance.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Transparency helps markets form expectations and strengthens policy transmission. Standards are only as effective as the compliance behind them, which the ROSCs assess.

self_check.prompt_text: Which standards did the IMF devise for data dissemination?
self_check.expected_takeaway: SDDS and GDDS.

items.title: Registering an NBFC and the types of NBFC
items.core_explanation_md:
**Conditions:** a **company** under the Companies Act; **Net Owned Fund Rs 2 crore**; **principal business financial**; at least one **director from the financial field**; **clean CIBIL records**.

**Types:** deposit accepting or **ND**; **NBFC-SI** (asset size Rs 100 crore or more); **NBFC-NDSI** are the non-deposit accepting systemically important ones.

**Other regulators:** **IRDA** (insurance), **NHB** (housing finance, in the courseware text), **SEBI** (brokers, merchant banks, mutual funds, venture capital, CIS), **State Governments** (chit funds), **MCA** (Nidhi).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Unlike banks, NBFCs are not governed by the Banking Regulation Act. A company outside the Reserve Bank's registration is regulated by the body that governs its activity.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the minimum Net Owned Fund for NBFC registration, as stated in this unit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Rs 2 crore.

items.title: The 11 NBFC categories by activity
items.core_explanation_md: **ICC** (lending and investment); **IFC** (infrastructure finance); **CIC** (group company holdings); **IDF** (long-term debt into mature infrastructure projects, **one year of satisfactory performance**); **MFI** (collateral free small ticket loans); **Factor** (receivables); **NOFHC** (promoters setting up new banks); **MGC** (mortgage guarantee); **AA** (consolidated financial information to the customer); **P2P** (online lender-borrower platform); **HFC** (housing finance).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The categories are defined by activity, so one NBFC fits one category. Account aggregators move data, not funds.

self_check.expected_takeaway: NBFC-NOFHC.

items.title: Growth and the Reserve Bank role
items.core_explanation_md:
**Growth:** NBFC assets grew at a **18.6 per cent CAGR** from March 2009 to March 2019 against **10.7 per cent** for scheduled commercial banks.

**Regulation:** under **Chapters III B, III C and V of the RBI Act, 1934**; **three-fold focus: depositor protection, consumer protection and financial stability**.

**Punitive powers:** **cancel the Certificate of Registration**, **prohibit deposit acceptance**, **criminal cases** or **winding up petitions**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The sector's interconnection with banks (most of its funds come from SCBs) is why stress can transmit between them. The RBI also promotes an SRO for NBFC-MFIs.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the three aims of NBFC regulation?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Depositor protection, consumer protection and financial stability.

items.title: Scale-based regulation and supervisory policies
items.core_explanation_md:
**Four layers:** **Base** (non-deposit taking, below Rs 1,000 crore), **Middle** (all deposit takers and Rs 1,000 crore and above), **Upper** (RBI-identified by parameters and scoring), **Top** (empty unless the RBI sees systemic risk); effective **1 October 2022**.

**Norms:** **CRAR 15 per cent**; **CET1 at least 9 per cent** for the upper layer; **single/group borrower exposure 25 / 40 per cent**; **NPA at more than 90 days overdue**; **Chief Compliance Officer** for upper and middle layers.

**PCA:** from **1 October 2022**; key parameters **CRAR, Tier I and net NPA**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The scale-based approach lets regulation grow with size and risk. HFCs came under the Reserve Bank from 9 August 2019.

self_check.prompt_text: Which layer is proposed to remain empty unless the RBI sees systemic risk?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The top layer.

items.title: Evolution and eligibility of primary dealers
items.core_explanation_md:
**Purpose:** widen the investor base, make the G-Sec market **liquid and broad-based**, develop **underwriting and market making**.

**History:** the **PD system began in 1995**; at **31 March 2021**: **21 PDs** (**14 bank departments, 7 standalone PDs**, SPDs registered as **NBFCs under Section 45 IA**).

**Authorisation:** apply to the **CGM, IDMD, RBI Mumbai**; **in principle approval**, then an **authorisation letter**; **undertaking** renewed **every three years**; **no step-down subsidiaries**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Authorisation depends on RBI's view of market needs and a clean record over the previous year. Continuation depends on compliance with the terms of authorisation.

items.title: Role of PDs and RBI liquidity support
items.core_explanation_md:
**Role:** primary auctions, market making, predominant G-Sec investment, **minimum success ratio**, efficient internal control.

**Liquidity support (SPDs):** **half shared equally** among SPDs; the other **50% split 1:1** between primary and secondary performance of the last six months; **weights 1 and 3** for T-Bill/CMB and G-Sec performance; limits revised **half-yearly**; priced at the **repo rate**; repay within **90 days**, else **Bank Rate + 5 percentage points**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The scheme rewards PDs that perform in both primary and secondary markets. It is available against eligible G-Secs including SDLs and is separate from LAF access.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The Repo Rate announced by the Reserve Bank.

items.title: Performance measures of PDs
items.core_explanation_md:
**Success ratio:** bids accepted ÷ bidding commitment, minimum **40 per cent** in T-Bill and CMB auctions, assessed **half-yearly**.

**Turnover ratio:** total purchase and sales ÷ average month-end stock; minimum **5 times** (outright and repo) and **3 times** (outright only) for dated securities; **10 times** and **6 times** for T-Bills/CMBs.

**Capital:** SPD CRAR mandated at **15 per cent**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: These ratios keep PDs active in both the primary and secondary market. The courseware tables of performance values are dated and are not taught here.

self_check.expected_takeaway: 5 times the average month-end stock.

items.title: Underwriting, bidding, secondary market and investment guidelines
items.core_explanation_md:
**Underwriting:** **MUC** (at least **50% of the notified amount**, shared equally) plus **ACU** auction (a PD cannot bid for more than **30%** of notified amount); RBI may accept up to **100%**; **devolvement** is set off against accepted ACU bids.

**SDLs:** PDs may underwrite up to **100%** collectively, **30%** per PD.

**T-Bills/CMBs:** yearly **bidding commitment**; **success ratio 40 per cent**; penal action on shortfall.

**Settlement:** funds in the current account by **3:00 pm** on the auction day; **SGL bouncing** if short; outright secondary trades **T+1** (FPIs and NDS-OM **T+2**).

**Investments:** at least **50%** of financial investments in G-Sec; G-Sec in **SGL or demat**; **HTM** up to **100% of audited NOF**, one transfer a year.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Banks running PD business departmentally apply the bank's own capital adequacy and risk framework. Auditors must certify compliance with the HTM instructions.

self_check.prompt_text: What share of the notified amount is the minimum underwriting commitment (MUC)?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At least 50 per cent, underwritten equally by all PDs.

items.title: IMF, IBRD and BIS
items.core_explanation_md:
**IMF:** Washington, D.C.; **Bretton Woods 1944**, formal in **1945**; roles: **surveillance, financial assistance, technical assistance**; facilities include **EFF, SFF, PRGF, Stand-by, CFF, Emergency Assistance, Exogenous Shock Facility**.

**IBRD:** loans to **middle income developing countries**; first of **five** World Bank Group institutions; concessional arm is the **IDA**.

**BIS:** **17 May 1930**, **Basel**; a **bank for central banks**; created the **BCBS** after **Herstatt (1974)**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Each institution has a different client: IMF serves balance of payments needs, IBRD funds development projects, and BIS serves central banks.

self_check.prompt_text: Where is the BIS headquartered?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Basel, Switzerland.

items.title: Overseas and IFSC operations of banks
items.core_explanation_md: The RBI instruction of **1 December 2022** lets foreign branches and subsidiaries of Indian banks and **AIFIs** (including those in **IFSCs such as GIFT City**) deal in products **not permitted domestically**, subject to **RBI conditions** and the **host regulator**. **Capital adequacy, exposure norms (including the Large Exposure Framework) and valuation** apply, and the parent follows the **more stringent** of home and host rules.
items.expanded_explanation_md: If RBI norms do not give the prudential treatment of a product, the parent seeks specific RBI guidance.

self_check.prompt_text: Whose prudential rule applies to an overseas product: home or host?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The more stringent of the two.

items.title: The central bank view of crypto currencies
items.core_explanation_md:
**Genesis:** **bitcoin** from **2008**, attributed to **Satoshi Nakamoto**, using **blockchain/DLT**.

**Courseware arguments:** a currency needs an **issuer** and the attributes of money; crypto is neither currency, asset nor instrument; it **bypasses KYC/AML/CFT**; stablecoins raise concern.

**Policy view:** the note concludes that a **ban** is perhaps the most advisable, with **taxation** (30 per cent on transfers) used to contain spread.
items.expanded_explanation_md: These are the courseware arguments and the policy position as stated by the note.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the four functions of money the note tests crypto against?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Medium of exchange, measure of value, store of value and standard of deferred payments.

items.title: Central bank digital currency
items.core_explanation_md:
**CBDC:** **digital form of fiat currency**, **issued by the central bank**, **promotes financial inclusion**; a **centralised** form that may not give **anonymity**.

**Design:** a **two-tier** scheme with the central bank at the core and private firms at the customer interface.

**India:** announced in the **budget for 2022**; **wholesale pilot 1 November 2022**; **retail pilot 1 December 2022**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: mCBDC arrangements could make cross-border payments better but raise currency substitution concerns.

self_check.prompt_text: When was the retail CBDC pilot launched?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 1 December 2022.

items.title: Sustainable finance survey
items.core_explanation_md:
The **SFG** survey (**January 2022**) found **inadequate board-level engagement**, no separate sustainability unit in most banks, **physical and transition risks** as main sources of climate risk, and **disclosures not aligned** with an international framework.

**Suggestions:** board oversight and ESG KPIs, integrate climate risk into risk management, align disclosures, mobilise green capital, build capacity, plan **net-zero** operations (COP26).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The survey informs how the RBI shapes its supervisory approach to climate risk.

self_check.prompt_text: Which two kinds of risk did banks see as the main climate-related sources?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Physical and transition risks.

items.title: Glossary extracts
items.core_explanation_md: **BIC:** **8 or 11 characters** (bank 4, country 2, location 2, branch 3 optional), **SWIFT** is the registration authority. **Bank Rate:** **Section 49** of the RBI Act, standard rate to **rediscount** eligible bills. **Call money:** **overnight** inter-bank lending. **Haircut:** market value **reduced by a percentage**. **Infinet:** **June 1999**, **VSAT**, hub at **IDRBT Hyderabad**. **Inflation targeting:** one **objective** of keeping inflation at a target or band.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The glossary covers many more terms; this batch itemises only these.

self_check.prompt_text: How many characters can a BIC have?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Eight or eleven.
